abstract: |
  As unionization has declined and social support systems have weakened, many large U.S. employers now operate Employee Hardship Funds (EHFs) — programs providing emergency cash grants to workers, funded substantially through worker donations. Despite operating at hundreds of firms, EHFs have received no scholarly attention. Drawing on three pre-registered studies, I provide the first systematic evidence on how workers perceive EHFs and how realistic program messaging shapes their attitudes and behavioral intentions. A national survey of retail workers finds that fewer than one in four identify an EHF at their employer, even though workers value EHFs highly once described. Survey experiments at Home Depot and Walmart show that EHF messages shift union vote intentions without improving workers' perceived financial security. At Home Depot, messages about its more generous, heavily promoted program reduced interest in unionization and increased job attachment, consistent with union substitution arguments. At Walmart, messages about its more modest program reduced opposition to unions and produced no job attachment effects, the opposite of presumed employer interests. EHFs are best understood as part of a bundle of employment practices that constitute workplace governance, not as isolated interventions.

Even as American labor unions and social support systems atrophy, firms across the U.S. are sponsoring Employee Hardship Funds (EHFs). EHFs provide emergency cash grants to employees when facing crises like house fires, crime victimization, or natural disasters. Although EHFs are employer-administered, funding comes substantially from donations solicited from workers themselves.  This hybrid "private welfare" structure distinguishes EHFs from standard workplace benefits and human resources practices on the one hand and "corporate social responsibility" (CSR) initiatives around charitable causes on the other. Despite their growing prevalence, documented below, EHFs have received almost no systematic attention.

Viewing EHFs from multiple perspectives suggests they could have a variety of effects on workers beyond the stated goal of improving financial resilience.  From one angle,  EHFs represent a contemporary form of welfare capitalism or, in modern parlance, strategic human resources.  They are employer-provided benefits that may foster attachment and offer a partial substitute for unions. EHFs may then reduce the willingness to support unionization.   

From another angle, EHFs incorporate elements of mutual aid in which workers pool resources to assist one another, a practice historically associated with labor unions and fraternal organizations.  Thus EHFs may induce greater attachment to coworkers.  

From a third perspective, EHFs appear as an employer-run charity similar to CSR initiatives, but directed inward, towards employees.  A large literature shows CSR programs can serve important governance functions including attracting and retaining workers, building organizational culture, and eliciting effort.  Thus, understanding how workers perceive and engage with EHFs, and what effects they have on workplace attachment and labor relations, carries both theoretical and practical significance.

Drawing on three pre-registered studies, I provide the first systematic evidence on EHFs and uncover surprising patterns.^[The study was pre-registered under osf.io/fhq93.  In appendix \@ref(app-PAP), I document where the execution, analysis, or reporting deviates from the pre-analysis plans.] Study 1 surveys 1,008 US retail workers nationally, revealing that workers highly value EHFs when explained, yet fewer than one in four report that their employer offers such programs. This disconnect between value and awareness suggests these programs may not function as the recruitment signals that standard CSR theory would predict.

Studies 2 and 3 present survey experiments with workers at Home Depot and Walmart, respectively, two large retailers with established but programmatically distinct EHFs.  I study how exposure to realistic EHF messaging affects attitudes and behavioral intentions. I find that treatment increases job attachment and shifts worker willingness to vote for unionization _without_ producing any detectable improvement in perceived financial security, the programs' stated purpose. These effects vary sharply across firms. At Home Depot, where the program is generous and heavily promoted, exposure increased attachment and reduced union support among previously unaware workers. At Walmart, where the program is minimal and weakly promoted, identically formatted messaging produced no attachment gains and _reduced opposition_ to unionization, contrary to presumed employer interests.

I interpret these divergent findings in light of perceived organizational support. Whether an EHF message generates loyalty depends on whether workers experience it as credible--consistent with how their employer already treats them and adequate to the need the program acknowledges. Home Depot's EHF appears to meet this bar. Walmart's appears to fall short and may instead highlight the gap between what the employer acknowledges workers need and what it provides. This account is consistent with the evidence, but the research design in this paper cannot rule out other possibilities.  

This paper makes three main contributions. First, I document EHFs as a widespread but largely unstudied employment practice, providing the first systematic evidence on worker awareness and engagement with these programs.  Second, I provide the first experimental evidence that employer-provided welfare programs can shape worker attitudes toward unionization.  Effects are context dependent. A generous, well-promoted program reduces union support, consistent with union substitution arguments.  But information about a program implemented in a cost-control culture produces reduced opposition to unions, suggesting that EHF effects depend on whether an EHF is complementary with the firm's broader employment practices.  Third, I show that workplace practices can generate loyalty and shape union attitudes without necessarily improving material circumstances, challenging assumptions about how benefits operate.  This paper is also an entry in the growing literature on labor relations in the retail industry where tens of millions of Americans work in low-wage and unstable jobs.

<!-- Normatively, EHFs are neither straightforwardly benevolent nor purely manipulative. EHFs may provide genuine emergency support and strengthen workplace community, or they may substitute symbolic gestures for meaningful security while discouraging collective action. They may backfire. The divergent effects at Home Depot and Walmart suggest these programs operate as context-dependent tools of labor relations management. -->

These findings matter for several audiences. For labor relations researchers, this paper establishes that EHFs can function as instruments of union avoidance operating through cultural signaling rather than threats, but these effects are not automatic. For labor practitioners, the findings suggest that the effectiveness of EHF messaging depends on whether workers experience it as consistent with their broader job conditions; inadequate programs may enhance rather than threaten organizing opportunities. For scholars of social policy and political economy, EHFs illustrate how private welfare arrangements fill gaps left by weakened public safety nets, raising normative questions about whether these programs serve worker interests or primarily function as low-cost governance tools. For managers and HR practitioners, a well-designed and promoted EHF can strengthen employee attachment as part of a bundle of other practices, but token programs risk highlighting inadequacy.

# EHFs in practice {#sec-ehf-bkgrnd}

Home Depot and Walmart are two of North America's largest retailers, employing approximately 420,000 and 1.6 million US workers respectively. They compete in product and labor markets, faced union campaigns, and influence retail industry standards and local labor markets [@wiltshireWalmartSupercentersMonopsony2023; @derenoncourtVoluntaryMinimumWages2025; @wartzmanStillBrokeWalmarts2022].

Both firms operate in a US labor market characterized by low levels of unionization, strained public welfare and social insurance systems, and precarious employment arrangements [@hackerGreatRiskShift2019; @naiduThereAnyFuture2022; @thelenAmericanPrecariatCapitalism2019; @weilFissuredWorkplace2014]. Economic precarity induces a "cognitive tax" that harms job performance [@meurisPriceFinancialPrecarity2018; @meurisHighCostLow2015; @leanaOrganizationalBehaviorWorking2012], providing one business case for employer engagement around these issues. These conditions make emergency cash assistance programs potentially valuable yet also make workers vulnerable to employer influence.

Against this backdrop, Home Depot has maintained the Homer Fund since 1999 while Walmart started the Associates in Critical Need Trust (ACNT) in 2001.  Both programs are set up as non-profit charities offering cash grants for employees facing emergency expenses.  The Homer Fund makes grants of up to \$10,000 while the Walmart fund makes grants of up to \$1,500.  Beyond simple generosity, the programs differ in multiple ways, including application procedures and the frequency with which a worker can receive a grant.   Both programs solicit (tax deductible) donations from both corporate and front-line employees.^[It is unclear how many front-line workers would itemize deductions and therefore see any tax benefit.  Higher-paid corporate employees and executives may, however.]  Grants to workers are tax-exempt under US law.

ACNT and Homer Fund are examples of Employee Hardship Funds. Despite operating at hundreds of large employers, EHFs remain almost entirely absent from academic research.^[@amorimScheduleUnpredictabilityHighCost2022; @reichWorkingRespectCommunity2018 are the only two peer-reviewed pieces mentioning EHFs of which I am aware.] A small practitioner literature offers testimonials and aggregate disbursement data but lacks systematic evidence on awareness rates, application patterns, approval rates, or effects on workers [@associationofdisasterrelieffundsandemployeehardshipfundsEnvironmentalScanDisaster2013; @employeerelieffundeducationgroupEnvironmentalScanDisaster2019;@aspeninstituteIlluminatingHiddenSafety2019; @rodriguezEmployeeHardshipFunds2020;@rodriguezEveryCompanyShould2020; @canaryStrengtheningSafetyNet2026]. This paper provides the first rigorous analysis.

There is no central registry for EHFs, but I have documented over 320 companies across multiple industries operating EHFs as of January 2025, including nine of the ten largest US retailers by revenue. Many employers outsource administration to third-party nonprofit partners. The largest of these third parties, the Employee Assistance Foundation (EAF), claimed over 400 corporate clients and distributed over \$86 million in grants in 2020.^[Additional information about EHF regulation and third-party providers, including revenue and grant growth, is collected in appendix \@ref(app-3rd).] 

EHFs expanded rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, with both new program adoption and increased usage among existing programs.  Levi Strauss & Co. reported a three-fold increase in applications to their EHF in 2020 [@rodriguezEveryCompanyShould2020], with another spike in applications once coronavirus emergency aid programs expired in the US.  Home Depot suspended fundraising from employees and expedited grant processing during the pandemic emergency. EAF reported a more than tenfold increase in grant applications relative to historical averages in the first two quarters of 2020 as well as 140 new client EHFs [@employeeassistancefoundationDecadeAssistanceOffering2022].   In May 2020, amid extensive criticism of its workplace safety practices, worker protests, and nascent union activity in its warehouse and fulfillment centers, Amazon launched its \$25 million EHF.^[Amazon shuttered the program in August 2022.]  

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-HfACNTcomps) zooms in on Home Depot's Homer Fund and Walmart's ACNT using data from IRS 990 forms.  In the left panel I report net assets for each firm's nonprofit foundations.^[For tax purposes, both Homer Fund and ACNT EHFs are part of the larger Home Depot and Walmart corporate foundations, respectively.]  Both corporate charities show strong growth from 2010, but Homer Fund is operating at more than double the ACNT's size.  The right panel looks at grants to domestic individuals, my preferred indicator of EHF activity.^[The larger foundations typically focus on disbursing grants to other nonprofit and community organizations, as opposed to individuals.  The Homer Fund website reported disbursing \$17 million in 2023 EHF grants whereas the Home Depot foundation 2023 IRS form 990 reports \$19.1 million in grants to individuals.]  The Homer Fund made \$15-25 million in annual grants between 2008 and 2022 whereas ACNT typically disbursed less than \$10 million, notwithstanding Walmart's much larger corporate presence.  The Homer Fund reported making a total of over \$267 million in grants to more than 183,000 individuals over its existence. ACNT claimed to have disbursed over \$142 million over its existence to over 145,000 workers.   

```{r fig-HfACNTcomps, fig.show="hold", out.width="50%", fig.cap ="EHF assets and grant activity at Home Depot and Walmart."}
temp<-here::here('2_code', "IRS_filings.R")
source(file = temp)
rm(temp)

net_assets_plot
grants_plot
```

EHFs vary across firms in virtually all programmatic aspects including longevity, eligibility, application procedures, grant generosity, funding structure, and administration. Although all EHFs involve mutual aid, firms vary in how they communicate about programs. Home Depot promotes aggressively through social media, YouTube, and donation drives. Walmart appears to invest far less in promotion. Several major retailers, including Home Depot, highlight their EHFs in their annual Environment, Social, and Governance (ESG) reports [@thehomedepotEnvironmentalSocialGovernance2023], indicating these firms view EHFs as part of their broader strategy.

EHFs are distinctive in two ways that make them particularly interesting for industrial relations research. First, they combine employer control with worker funding---employers create the infrastructure but workers are asked to provide money, creating a hybrid of corporate welfare and peer mutual aid. Second, EHFs can extend to contingent workers excluded from traditional benefits, potentially serving as a flexible governance tool in fissured employment relationships. There are examples consistent with this interpretation. Amazon restricted its EHF to "Amazon Flex Delivery Partners, Delivery Service Partner Delivery Associates, Temporary Associates employed by eligible staffing agencies, and drivers of eligible line haul partners," i.e., non-standard, temporary contract labor.  EAF updated its EHF program guidelines, recommending that employers "include contractors, furloughed employees, and franchise employees" in their EHF schemes [@employeeassistancefoundationDecadeAssistanceOffering2022].

# Understanding EHFs: welfare capitalism, mutual aid, and contemporary labor relations {#sec-lit-review}

Employee Hardship Funds blend elements from three distinct but intersecting literatures: employer-sponsored welfare capitalism, worker mutual aid, and corporate social responsibility as a governance mechanism.  Situating EHFs in these traditions generates empirical expectations.

## Welfare capitalism and employer-provided benefits

EHFs can be viewed as a contemporary iteration of welfare capitalism.  In the early 20th Century, some employers provided workers significant amenities beyond wages---housing, healthcare, recreation, religious instruction, and emergency assistance---to attract and retain labor and forestall unionization [@brandesAmericanWelfareCapitalism1976;@jacobyModernManorsWelfare1998]. The logic is straightforward: when benefits are tied to continued employment, they increase switching costs and strengthen attachment.  By the interwar period, several large industrial firms created employer-sponsored "company unions" that substituted for independent unions' social and mutual aid functions but lacked any independent voice around wages, staffing, and benefits [@brandesAmericanWelfareCapitalism1976]. 

Even today, firms routinely use compensation strategically to preempt union organizing, producing the union "threat effect" [@farberNonunionWageRates2005; @taschereau-dumouchelUnionThreat2020].  Beyond wages, an older literature also at looked how "high performance work systems" and "strategic human resources practices" displace support for unionization [@kochanEffectsCorporateStrategy1986; @fioritoHumanResourceManagement2001].

One way to view EHFs is as an extension of this tradition, but with minimal employer expenditure and risk.  Unlike higher wages and incentive pay schemes or the company housing of historical welfare capitalism, EHFs represent limited and manageable costs. Significant EHF funding comes from tax-deductible worker donations, and programs scale flexibly. This makes EHFs an attractive governance tool. They appear to address worker needs while maintaining employer control and requiring only modest financial commitment. EHFs differ, however in that these programs do not bind workers to the employer in the same way as company housing or unvested equity. Attachment gains should be a combination of employer signalling and employer-mediated peer solidarity. 

## Mutual aid and worker solidarity

In EHFs, workers donate money that is then distributed to fellow workers in crisis. This structure evokes the long tradition of worker mutual aid in which workers pool resources to assist one another during hardship [@beitoMutualAidWelfare2000; @glennUnderstandingMutualBenefit2001; @dreyfusLabourMovementMutual1993]. Historically, workers themselves created and controlled mutual aid organizations.  These organizations coalesced around shared occupation, religion, or ethnicity and created dense social networks [@ismayTrustStrangersFriendly2018]. Many evolved into labor unions [@webbHistoryTradeUnionism1920; @bacharachMutualAidUnion2018; @jarleyUnionsSocialCapital2005] or served as organizing structures when unions were suppressed [@morrisCriminalConspiracyEarly1937; @blochVoluntaryAssociationsCorporate2017]. Unions continue to maintain emergency aid programs and insurance schemes to recruit, retain, and support members [@hertel-fernandezWhyPublicSector2021]. 

EHFs differ fundamentally from traditional mutual aid. Workers neither organize nor direct EHFs and, in most programs, need not donate to be eligible for benefits. EHFs are employer-specific, lacking the cross-firm networks that characterized fraternal organizations. And EHFs do not build organizational capacity among workers. Some programs (including the Homer Fund) require applicants to get the support of their supervisor, embedding aid-seeking in hierarchical relationships rather than horizontal networks.  Nevertheless, EHFs appropriate the rhetoric and structure of mutual aid and may connect with the same "social custom" motivations associated with unions [@naylorEconomicTheoryOpen1993].

As a worker-funded benefit pool, EHFs may foster a sense of mutual support and solidarity with co-workers which may help build a "community of fate" and make union appeals more attractive [@ahlquistInterestOthersOrganizations2013]. This require that workers attribute the program and its benefits to their own collective action.  Alternatively, the literature on welfare capitalism and individual union support suggests that if workers attribute EHFs to employer benevolence, if EHFs substitute for union benefits, or if EHFs increase job satisfaction, EHFs would reduce support for unionization [@mcclendonIndividualDecisionUnionize1998].  The structural features of EHFs favor the welfare capitalism union substitution effect.   

## CSR and job attachment

EHFs are formally charitable entities to which both corporate and front-line employees donate.  As such, they connect with a large literature linking CSR initiatives with worker attitudes and behavior. Research distinguishes between external (charitable donations, environmental commitments, community voluntarism) and internal (HR practices, employee training and well-being programs)  CSR programs [@brammerContributionCorporateSocial2007a; @hawnMindGapInterplay2016; @elakremiHowEmployeesPerceive2018].  EHFs, as internal CSR, clearly shade into HR and labor relations practices.
  
A substantial body of research demonstrates a business case for CSR initiatives.  CSR programs attract value-aligned workers and reduce the wages required to attract high performers [@brekkeAttractingResponsibleEmployees2008; @greeningCorporateSocialPerformance2000; @turbanCorporateSocialPerformance1997; @jonesWhyAreJob2014; @burbanoSocialResponsibilityMessages2016; @wilmersValuesInequalityProsocial2022a].  CSR can increase worker identification with the firm [@ruppEmployeeReactionsCorporate2006; @brammerContributionCorporateSocial2007a], strengthen attachment to coworkers [@bodeCorporateSocialInitiatives2015], and reduce turnover [@portocarreroEffectsShortTermCorporate2024]. Experiments in labs and online labor markets find that information about employer charitable activities increases worker productivity [@toninCorporatePhilanthropyProductivity2015], elicits unpaid effort [@burbanoGettingGigWorkers2021; @cassarJobMissionSubstitute2019], and reduces willingness to engage in misconduct [@burbanoMitigatingGigRemote2022].  

These findings link CSR with the broader notion of "perceived organizational support", in which workers attribute coherent intentions and values to complex organizations [@eisenbergerPerceivedOrganizationalSupport2020]. They look to past treatment, HR practices, and work conditions as signals about how much their employer values them.  EHF programs, forming part of this matrix, can increase perceived support and therefore job attachment.   

But it can work the other way. When CSR initiatives are inconsistent with other organizational practices or when managerial motives are perceived as insincere, workers interpret CSR as cynical and instrumental, undermining the program.  Job attachment effects weaken or reverse [@burbanoMitigatingGigRemote2022; @cassarIntentionsDoingGood2021; @doniaCSRAnyOther2019; @chengImpactCSRPerceptions2022; @amengualTrueMotivesProsocial2021; @gatignon-turnauMisUsingEmployeeVolunteering2015]. Far from passively accepting managerial initiatives, workers actively evaluate whether these programs credibly demonstrate organizational support.  

CSR initiatives, as part of a bundle of workplace practices, connects with models of union support. Demand for unionization originates with "a gap between expectations and achievements as to job-related outcomes relating to material resources..., social dominance (respect), or job security." [@mcclendonIndividualDecisionUnionize1998, 37-38]  An EHF viewed as insincere signals disrespect and highlights dominance. To the extent an EHF is inconsistent with other practices it could signal a lack of organizational support, engendering an increased interest in unionization, rather than the reverse.  

## Research questions and hypotheses
These literatures suggest several lines of inquiry, but also areas of uncertainty where empirical evidence is especially valuable. I frame these research questions as testable hypotheses.

- **H1 (Financial Security):** Employers state that EHFs are designed to increase the financial resilience of their workforce. @haushoferEconomicPsychologicalEffects2020 document a "peace of mind effect" in which the mere presence of a modest insurance scheme reduces stress, even if the program goes unused.  Thus exposure to EHF messaging should enhance EHF awareness and improve workers' sense of financial security.

- **H2 (Awareness):** If EHFs are tools for attracting and retaining value-aligned workers (as CSR theory suggests), then employers should promote them widely and there should be broad awareness among workers about EHF programs at their own employer (retention) and at competing firms (attraction).  Evidence for this hypothesis will be observational, not experimental.

- **H3 (Attachment):** Both welfare capitalism and CSR literatures predict that workplace benefits and CSR programs increase job attachment. EHFs combine both elements. EHF messages should strengthen job attachment.

- **H4 (Unionization):** The welfare capitalism literature generates the hypothesis that EHFs should reduce union support by providing benefits that unions might otherwise secure while also appropriating the language of mutual aid. The mutual aid structure may, however, increase receptivity to unions insofar as workers attribute the program to their co-workers over the employer.

- **H5 (Contingency):** Strategic HR and CSR research suggest that EHF effects depend on perceived authenticity and consistency with other organizational practices.  A discordant or token EHF program may create an expectations gap that undermines the EHF's effects or even enhances interest in unionization.  Thus programs that are more generous, heavily promoted, and better integrated into existing HR practices and culture should produce stronger effects than token programs.

<!-- Table \@ref(tab:tab-hypotheses) summarizes these hypotheses for ease of reference.  -->

Note that H1-H4 represent predictions from existing theory applied to the EHF context. H4 acknowledges potentially conflicting predictions. In the context of this paper's research design, H2 and H5 rely on observational evidence only.  H5 is a boundary condition suggested by prior research. With data from two firms, I can demonstrate whether effects differ between firms with different EHF characteristics, a descriptive quantity.

```{r tab-hypotheses, eval = FALSE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, results='asis'}
#library(kableExtra)
#library(tibble)

hypotheses <- tribble(
  ~"Hypothesis", ~"Description",
  "H1", "Exposure to EHF messaging improves subjective financial security.",
  "H2", "Workers should be aware of both their employer's EHF and those at other major employers.",
  "H3", "Exposure to EHF messaging increases workers’ job attachment.",
  "H4", "Exposure to EHF messaging reduces support for unionization.",
  "H5", "The effects of EHF messaging on job attachment and union support are contingent on program design and integration."
)

hypotheses %>%
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Summary of empirical hypotheses",
      label = "tab-hypotheses",  # This is the LaTeX label
    escape = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), 
    full_width = FALSE) |> 
  column_spec(2, width = "10cm")  # Adjust width as needed
```

# Study populations and measurement

Worker surveys are the most direct approach for establishing an empirical baseline for EHFs.   In this paper I focus on retail workers. Retail employs over 16 million Americans, making it one of the largest US employment sectors. Nine of the ten largest US retailers maintain EHFs, yet no research has examined worker awareness or attitudes toward these programs. If EHFs function as governance tools or recruitment mechanisms, workers in this competitive, high-turnover industry should be aware of them. The industry's low wages, limited benefits, and recent unionization campaigns make it an ideal context for studying EHFs as governance tools.

## Measuring key quantities 

Here I outline the measurement strategies for key quantities across all three studies.  I note additional details and study-specific differences below where necessary.  Extensive detail, justification, and supplementary measurement analysis appears in Appendix \@ref(app-measurement).  All ordered categorical variables are scaled to the $[0,1]$ interval.

### EHF awareness and engagement

Across all three studies the primary way I measure _EHF awareness_ is by embedding "emergency cash assistance to help in unexpected hard times" in a list of potential job amenities.  Respondents then select all the items on the list that pertain to their retail job.  This approach minimizes demand effects and avoids contaminating the survey experiments in Studies 2 and 3. 

Later in Study 1, after explaining EHFs, I also ask directly whether respondents had heard of such programs and whether their employer had one.^[
The question wording was "Some companies offer their employees programs called "Employee Hardship Funds". Employee Hardship Funds provide emergency cash to a company's workers if they face unexpected financial hardships, such as a house or apartment fire. The emergency money from the Employee Hardship Fund is not a loan and does not have to be repaid. The money in the fund comes directly from donations from the company's own workers. Before taking this survey, had you ever heard of Employee Hardship Funds?"] In Study 1, both the list-based and direct questions capture worker perceptions only; I cannot confirm the accuracy of their reports about their employers' EHFs in Study 1.

By way of EHF engagement, Study 1 asked respondents how much they would be willing to donate to an EHF.  Study 2 and Study 3 asked respondents whether they have ever _applied_ to, _donated_ to, and _received_ a grant from their employer's EHF program.  We also asked respondents whether they personally _know_ a coworker who has received an EHF grant. In study 3 I offer respondents an opportunity to click through to donate to their employer's EHF as a behavioral indicator of engagement.

### Outcomes

In the main text, I measure _subjective financial security_ by adapting the Federal Reserve's standard question from the Survey of Household Economics and Decision-making question [@boardofgovernorsofthefederalreservesystemEconomicWellBeingHouseholds2023]: "How confident are you that you could come up with \$400 if an unexpected need arose within the next month?" The responses on a 4-point scale range from "certain I could not" to "certain I could". This widely-used indicator of subjective financial resilience asks about exactly the type of emergency hardships that EHFs claim to address [@groverWhat400Emergency2021]. 

I use multiple indicators of _job attachment_:

* Loyalty to coworkers (4-point scale, "none at all" to "a lot")
* Loyalty to employer (same scale)
* Willingness to recommend employer (5-point scale, "definitely would not recommend" to "certainly would recommend")
* Quit intentions (Studies 1 and 3 only; 5-point scale from "not at all likely" to "extremely likely", reverse-scaled)

For concision, I express these variables as a job attachment index where higher scores indicate greater job attachment.^[I conducted exploratory factor analysis on these items in all three samples. Results showed a single dominant factor explaining 64% (Study 2) and 54% (Study 3) of variance. Internal consistency reliability was acceptable (Cronbach's $\alpha$ = 0.84 at Home Depot and 0.81 at Walmart). Following the pre-registered plan, I used factor scores on this unique factor as the job attachment index. Appendix \@ref(app-attachmentindex) provides complete psychometric details including factor loading, reliability statistics, and convergent/discriminant validity evidence. Results analyzing individual items separately for the experiments (Appendix \@ref(app-cov) and \@ref(app-full-wmt)) show consistent treatment effects across all components, supporting the composite index approach.]

For measuring _union support_ at the current job, I use the standard union vote intention question from industrial relations research [@kochanWorkerVoiceAmerica2019; @ahlquistRiseUnionCurious2024; @freemanWhatUnions1984; @fioritoHumanResourceManagement2001; @premackIndividualUnionizationDecisions1988]: "If an election were held today to decide whether employees like you should be represented by a union at [EMPLOYER], would you vote for the union or against the union?" Responses are in \{for the union, against the union, not sure\}.  In Study 3 only, I also asked: "What percent of your coworkers do you think would vote FOR a union if there were an election today?" (0-100 scale). This captures perceptions of collective support distinct from personal voting intentions. 

The union vote question taps a concrete behavioral intention, not an abstract attitude.  The question reflects the union certification voting process in the US, giving it strong face validity.  Actual pro-union voting is strongly related to stated vote intentions in this questions [@premackIndividualUnionizationDecisions1988].  

In analyzing the union vote intention questions and in line with pre-registered plans, I am careful to retain respondents who answer "don't know". Some models of voting in union elections suggest the undecided are most responsive to the opinions of coworkers but perhaps harder to mobilize to turnout  [@summersVotingUnionsDecision1986].  "Don't know" respondents express views between those of committed supporters and opponents of unionization;  abstention for a union election is viewed as substantively important in its own right [@hepburnVoteNotVote2001].  @ahlquistRiseUnionCurious2024 provide evidence that that the "don't know" responses for this question reflect actual ambivalence, rather than survey satisficing.  I replicate their approach in Studies 1 and 3: those answering "not sure" were then probed as to whether they "lean" toward yes or no; 75% and 88% of those respondents, respectively,  were adamant about their "don't know" response.

# Study 1: Observational evidence on EHF awareness and attitudes among US retail workers {#sec-study-1}

Despite operating at hundreds of large employers, EHFs remain unstudied. Do workers know these programs exist? Do they value them? Study 1 provides the first systematic evidence on worker awareness, engagement, and preferences.

For Study 1, I surveyed US retail workers through the CloudResearch panel in February 2025.  Recruitment targeted US residents 18 and older employed in retail.  All surveys were conducted online and the sample was restricted to those who confirmed current retail employment and passed attention checks, producing `r nrow(genpop)` valid responses.^[Respondents with non-US or duplicate IP addresses reporting identical demographic values were also excluded.]  I constructed post-stratification weights using 2024 American Community Survey data for retail workers to mitigate some potential selection bias.^[Weights adjust for gender, race, and education to match the employed retail workforce nationally. All descriptive statistics reported below use weighted calculations.] Sample demographic descriptions appear in Appendix \@ref(app-genpop-survsum), but I note that the unweighted sample was diverse (37% non-white, 51% male) and largely comprised of hourly workers (83%).

## Descriptive findings

**Finding 1: low awareness of EHF programs**
```{r genpop-awareness-calcs, echo=FALSE}
genpop_aware_tab<- genpop_w |> summarise(
          got.ehf.prop = survey_mean(emerg_assist_benefits=="Yes", 
                                         na.rm=TRUE),
          aware.prior.prop = survey_mean(ehf_prior_know=="Yes", na.rm=T),
          claim.ehf.prop = survey_mean(ehf_own_comp == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE)
          #know.prop = survey_mean(HF_know=="Yes", na.rm=T),  # too many NAs
          #applied.prop = survey_mean(HF_applied=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         #received.prop = survey_mean(HF_received=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         #donated.prop = survey_mean(HF_donate=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         #eligible.prop = survey_mean(Q4.2=="Yes", na.rm=T),
          )



genpop_joint <- update(
  genpop_w,
  got   = emerg_assist_benefits == "Yes",
  claim = ehf_own_comp == "Yes"
)

got_claim <- genpop_joint %>%
  svyttest(
    design = .,
    formula = got - claim ~ 0,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
```

Using the list-based question approach, I find that `r round(100*genpop_aware_tab$got.ehf.prop)`% (se = `r round(100*genpop_aware_tab$got.ehf.prop_se)`%) report that their current employer offers emergency cash assistance. When asked directly after EHFs are explained, `r round(100*genpop_aware_tab$claim.ehf.prop)`% (se = `r round(100*genpop_aware_tab$claim.ehf.prop_se)`%) claim their employer has such a program ($p =$ `r round(got_claim$p.value,2)` for the difference).  For context, `r round(100*genpop_aware_tab$aware.prior.prop)`% (se = `r round(100*genpop_aware_tab$aware.prior.prop_se)`%) said that they had heard of EHF programs prior to taking the survey. In a separate, Fall 2022 survey of front-line workers in five industries (including retail), only 13% of retail workers reported that their employer had an emergency cash grant program using a similar elicitation method [@ahlquist2022WERNWorkers2025].^[See Appendix \@ref(app-wern) for more information on this supplementary survey.]  Low levels of internal awareness, while perhaps contradicting retention-oriented CSR mechanisms, may still be consistent EHFs as a recruiting signal in a high-turnover environment.

In Study 1 respondents were asked whether they believed specific large retail employers had EHFs.^[The employers were Costco (no), Disney (yes), Home Depot (yes), Kohl's (yes), Starbucks (yes), Walmart (yes).] Figure \@ref(fig:fig-genpop-beliefs) shows their answers, broken out by whether the respondent believes their own employer has an EHF program. Regardless of whether a respondent believes their own employer has an EHF, large majorities express ignorance about programs at major employers. Even for Walmart and Home Depot, which have operated EHFs for over 20 years, fewer than 30% of workers correctly identified these firms as having programs.

```{r fig-genpop-beliefs, fig.show="hold", out.width="80%", fig.cap="Worker beliefs about EHFs at major US retailers, by own employer EHF status"}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'general_retail', '6_awareness_amenities_models_plots_gp.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)

genpop_engage_sum<- genpop_w |> 
  summarize(donte_new = survey_mean(ehf_donate_new!="I would not donate at all",
                            na.rm=TRUE),
         donte_exist = survey_mean(ehf_donate_exist=="Yes",
                            na.rm=TRUE),
         union_support = survey_mean(union_elec=="For the union", na.rm=T),
         union_oppose = survey_mean(union_elec=="Against the union", na.rm=T),
         wage_med = survey_median(pph, na.rm=T)
  )

ehf_firm_beliefs
```

Workers who report that their own employer has an EHF are somewhat more likely to correctly identify programs at other retailers, but knowledge still remains limited. If EHFs served as significant tools for attracting value-aligned workers, I would expect much higher awareness EHFs at competing firms. EHFs operate with low salience in retail labor markets.  I fail to find support for H2 (awareness).

**Finding 2: Strong interest in EHFs...once explained**

Despite limited awareness, workers respond enthusiastically when EHFs are explained. After providing a description of an EHF, I asked about their current employer's program and their level of support. Of workers whose employer has an EHF `r round(100*support_sum$prop[1])`%  are 'extremely supportive' of maintaining it, and `r round(100*support_sum$prop[4])`% of those without one strongly support creating one ($p =$ `r round(tt$p.value,2)` for difference).  

I asked about willingness to donate to an EHF, `r round(100*genpop_engage_sum$donte_new)`% would donate, if their employer created an EHF, with the modal response being "regular donations of less than \$20." While this is aspirational rather than documented behavior, it suggests that workers see value in pooling resources to help coworkers.  

```{r fig-genpop-support, eval=FALSE, fig.show="hold", out.width="80%", fig.cap="Worker support for creating (R) or maintaining (L) an EHF at current job."}
ehf_support_genpop
```

**Finding 3: EHFs valued as a job amenity**

As a simple assessment for how workers value EHFs, I presented a hypothetical job scenario and a series of potential job amenities:

> "Imagine another retailer was hiring, paying the same wage you are earning at [Employer].  The new job has a commute that is 10 minutes longer but has better benefits.  How seriously would you consider this offer, if the better benefits were [Benefit]?"

I then asked respondents to rate their interest in the hypothetical job (not at all seriously, somewhat seriously, very seriously).  Note that I did not ask respondents to rank these benefits or otherwise make tradeoffs.

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-genpop-prefs) shows results. "Emergency cash offered during hard times" ranks second only to paid time off in generating very serious interest in switching employers. Notably, EHFs receive higher average ratings than parental leave or union representation. At median hourly wages in the sample (\$16/hour), the additional 20-minute daily commute implies forgoing approximately `r paste("$",round(1/3*genpop_engage_sum$wage_med,2), sep="")` in earnings per round trip to work.^[I focused on difference in commute time rather than a difference in hourly wage rates because shift availability and scheduling practices are highly variable within and across retailers [@harknettImprovingHealthEconomic2021;@schneiderHardTimesRoutine2021].] That workers would seriously consider this trade off for an EHF suggests they perceive substantial value in these programs, even though many are unaware whether their current employer already offers one.

```{r fig-genpop-prefs, fig.show="hold", out.width="80%", fig.cap="Degree of interest in a new job with longer commute but better amenities."}
amenity_plot_w_gp
```

**Finding 4: workers want a voice in the EHF**

Finally, I ask workers how they would structure an EHF. Using a 5-point scale ranging from complete employer control to complete worker control, I asked respondents who did not report an EHF at their current retail job how much control workers _should_ have if their employer launched an EHF program.  Workers overwhelming want a voice in the EHF; only `r round(100*control_sum$prop[1])`% want complete employer control. The modal response is a shared governance model with input from both the employer and workers, with over 75% preferring an EHF arrangement in which workers have at least as much control as management.   

This finding aligns with other evidence of significant latent worker demand for voice over workplace decisions [@mazumderWhatAmericansWant2024; @kochanWorkerVoiceAmerica2019]. It also suggests tension between how workers would prefer EHFs to operate (participatory mutual aid) and how they typically function (employer-controlled programs).

```{r fig-genpop-control, eval=FALSE, fig.show="hold", out.width="80%", fig.cap= "Workers' preferred locus of EHF control"}
genpop_ehf_cntrl
```

## Discussion

Study 1 reveals a puzzle: workers value emergency assistance yet remain largely unaware of EHFs. If employers were using EHFs to attract value-aligned workers in a high-turnover industry, as the CSR literature suggests, awareness about programs at major employers should be far higher.^[Appendix \@ref(app-genpop-est) reports basic regressions linking reported EHF with job attachment and union vote intentions in the cross-sectional survey.]

Several mechanisms might explain low awareness. Turnover may be so rapid that workers never get a chance to learn about the EHF; I investigate tenure-linked awareness growth in Studies 2 and 3.  Simultaneously, low employer investment in promotion and outreach, as in the case of Walmart's relatively modest efforts, could account for low awareness. Workers may simply fail to retain the information if they don't anticipate needing emergency funds.

# Studies 2 \& 3: experimental evidence from Home Depot and Walmart {#sec-study-2-3}

Study 1 documented that retail workers are largely unaware of EHF programs but value them when explained. Studies 2 and 3 expose workers  to realistic EHF messages, examining whether the message affects worker financial security, attachment to the workplace, and attitudes toward unionization.  By concentrating on specific firms, I can evaluate the accuracy of workers' EHF knowledge while also producing context-specific survey experiments. To make recruiting a survey sample feasible, I only consider extremely large employers. 

The selection of Home Depot and Walmart reflects two complementary goals. I selected Home Depot as an "extreme case" [@seawrightCaseSelectionTechniques2008].  Based on interviews with EHF practitioners and the applied literature, Home Depot operates one of the oldest, most generous, and most heavily promoted EHF programs anywhere. Home Depot is where any EHF effect is most likely to be detectable. I selected Walmart to explore heterogeneity and boundary conditions across firms facing similar competitive conditions. 

Home Depot and Walmart are matched on the dimensions likely to confound comparisons, namely industry, national scale, program age, and in-house EHF management.  But they differ substantially in EHF program characteristics. While resembling a "most similar" case design, it is not one in any strict sense: Walmart and Home Depot also differ on other dimension such as workforce composition and organizational culture. With only two firms and cross-sectional surveys, I cannot isolate which of these factors explains divergent results. The two-firm comparison can establish a more modest but valuable descriptive finding: whether EHF effects are consistently detectable across contexts, and whether any differences are directionally consistent with H5.

## Program characteristics

Home Depot operates the Homer Fund, established in 1999. The program offers grants up to \$10,000 per qualifying event with day-one eligibility and no limits on repeat applications. In fiscal year 2022 (the year of the survey), the Homer Fund distributed \$21.2 million to over 12,000 workers [@thehomedepotEnvironmentalSocialGovernance2023], or about \$1750 per grant.

Home Depot actively promotes the program through social media, YouTube, donation drives, and integration into corporate social responsibility messaging. Store locations compete in fundraising campaigns. The Homer Fund claims that a "majority of contributions" come from front-line associates, emphasizing the mutual aid component.^[ [https://corporate.homedepot.com/page/homer-fund-0](https://corporate.homedepot.com/page/homer-fund-0) ] @sullMeasuringCultureLeading2019, using online postings to develop measures of corporate culture, rank Home Depot at the 77th percentile for "collaboration" and 48th percentile for "respect", relatively among retailers.  Home Depot corporate employees and executives are required to work a quarterly 8-hour retail shift [@heinzlHomeDepotOrders2024].

Walmart operates the Associates in Critical Need Trust (ACNT), established in 2001. The program offers a maximum \$1,500 in total grants over a rolling five-year period, regardless of qualifying events.  ACNT eligibility requires at least 90 days of employment tenure. In recent years, ACNT distributed under \$10 million annually despite Walmart employing nearly four times as many US workers as Home Depot. Walmart provides minimal promotion---no dedicated videos, limited social media presence, and no evidence of donation drives comparable to Home Depot's.^[Interestingly, Walmart matches employee donations to the Walmart political action committee 2:1 with corporate donations to the ACNT. In 2015, the Federal Election Commission rejected a challenge to this practice.  In the sample, fewer than 1% of respondents reported making a contribution to the Walmart PAC.] Walmart's corporate culture ranks at the 15th percentile for respect and 37th percentile for collaboration [@sullMeasuringCultureLeading2019]. The firm is known for cost control rather than investment in employees [@cascioDecencyMeansMore2006; @wartzmanStillBrokeWalmarts2022; @reichWorkingRespectCommunity2018], notwithstanding a recent push to raise compensation through a "voluntary minimum wage" [@derenoncourtVoluntaryMinimumWages2025].
 
Table \@ref(tab:tab-ehf-comparison) summarizes these differences. Under H5, I expect stronger effects at Home Depot, where the program is more generous and appears more consistent with the broader workplace culture.

```{r tab-ehf-comparison, echo=FALSE}

  Feature = c("Established", "Maximum grant", "Eligibility", 
              "Repeat grants", "Annual disbursements (2022)", 
              "US employees (approx.)", "Grants per employee",

                 "Collaboration, teamwork, expertise",

  Walmart = c("2001", "$1,500 (5-year max)", "after 90 days",
              "No (5-year cap)", "<$10 million",
              "1,600,000", "~$6/employee",
              "Low",
              "Cost control, efficiency",
              "37 %ile (collaboration), 15 %ile (respect)",
              "In-house")
)

kable(ehf_comparison,
      col.names = c("Feature", "Home Depot (Homer Fund)", "Walmart (ACNT)"),
      caption = "EHF Program Characteristics Comparison",
      booktabs = TRUE,
      longtable = TRUE)# %>%
  #kable_styling(
    #latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped", "scale_down"),font_size = 10) %>%
  #column_spec(1, width = "3cm") %>%
  #column_spec(2, width = "5.5cm") %>%
```

## Respondent recruitment and sample description 

I recruited participants independently for each firm using targeted Meta advertising (Facebook, Instagram, Threads), a method validated for recruting  retail workers into surveys [@schneiderWhatFacebookTool2019; @growFacebooksAdvertisingData2022]. Ads targeted US users aged 18+ whom Meta identified as employees of Home Depot or Walmart. Those included in the analysis confirmed current employment at Home Depot or Walmart, passed attention checks, and were randomly assigned to experimental conditions. Those completing the survey entered a raffle for prizes. While this produces some selection bias relative to a hypothetical random sample, the method has been shown to perform well in similar contexts [@schneiderWhatFacebookTool2019; @zhangQuotaSamplingUsing2020; @neundorfHowImproveRepresentativeness2023]. Critically, targeted social media recruitment is the best, cost-effective method for generating large matched worker-employer samples in the US.

The initial survey, Study 2 (Home Depot), was fielded September–October 2021 ($N=515$). Study 3 (Walmart) was in the field October–December 2024 ($N=980$). The three-year gap reflects funding constraints; I address timing concerns in detail below. Both samples are almost entirely hourly workers with average age 47 and over 75% white. The Home Depot sample is 56% male; Walmart is 78% female. Following @schneiderWhatFacebookTool2019, I construct raking weights using Meta-reported age and gender distributions for users employed at each firm. Weights are used for descriptive statistics but not experimental analysis. Full demographic details appear in Appendices \@ref(app-survsum-uw) and \@ref(app-wmt-survsum).

```{r summary-calcs, echo=FALSE}
summary_tab_uw<-summarise(THD_comp_uw, 
          male = mean(male, na.rm=T), 
          age = median(rk_age, na.rm=T),

          antiunion = table(THD_comp_uw$union_vote)["Against the union"]/sum(!is.na(THD_comp_uw$union_vote))
          )

          nonwhite = mean(nonwhite, na.rm=T),
          prounion = table(cntrls$union_vote)["For the union"]/sum(!is.na(cntrls$union_vote)),
          antiunion = table(cntrls$union_vote)["Against the union"]/sum(!is.na(cntrls$union_vote))
          )

cntrls_svy <- subset(THD_comp, HDTreatment == "cntrl")

summary_tab_c <- cntrls_svy |>
  summarise(
    male      = survey_mean(male, na.rm = TRUE),
    age       = survey_median(rk_age, na.rm = TRUE),
```

## EHF awareness and engagement

Before presenting experimental results, I establish baseline awareness rates and identify which respondents were already exposed to EHF information before treatment (the "pre-exposed"). This is critical because pre-exposed workers may respond differently to EHF messages than those learning for the first time [@druckmanLearningMorePolitical2012a].^[I use the terms "aware" and "pre-exposed" interchangeably.] I measured awareness using the list-based approach discussed above.^[In Appendix \@ref(app-HFaware), I discuss two other indicators of awareness and compare them with the preferred "list" measure.] This pre-treatment measure of EHF awareness is available for all survey respondents without contaminating the survey experiment.
      
```{r awareness-calcs, echo=FALSE}
aware_tab<-summarise(THD_comp, 
          aware.prop.l = survey_mean(EHF_aware_list), 
          aware.prop.s = survey_mean(EHF_aware_simp=="Yes", na.rm=T),
          know.prop = survey_mean(HF_know=="Yes", na.rm=T),  # too many NAs
          applied.prop = survey_mean(HF_applied=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         received.prop = survey_mean(HF_received=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         donated.prop = survey_mean(HF_donate=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         eligible.prop = survey_mean(Q4.2=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         tenure = survey_mean(tenure_num, na.rm=T),
         tenure.sd = survey_sd(tenure_num, na.rm=T)
          )
takeup <- THD_comp |> 
  filter(HDTreatment != "cntrl", Q4.2 == "Yes") |> 
  summarize(takeup.prop = survey_mean(HF_applied == "Yes"))

aware_tab_uw<-summarise(THD_comp_uw, 
          aware.prop.l = mean(EHF_aware_list), 
          aware.prop.s = mean(EHF_aware_simp=="Yes", na.rm=T),
          know.prop = mean(HF_know=="Yes", na.rm=T),  # too many NAs
          applied.prop = mean(HF_applied=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         received.prop = mean(HF_received=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         donated.prop = mean(HF_donate=="Yes", na.rm=T)
          )


#sum(grepl("Cash", THD_comp$Q2.15, fixed=T))/sum(!is.na(THD_comp$Q2.15)) #.61 unweighted
#svymean(~grepl("Cash", THD_comp$Q2.15, fixed=T),THD_dgn, na.rm=TRUE) # .61 weighted
#summary(as.factor(THD_comp$Q3.10))  #~85% awareness, unweighted
#svymean(~factor(THD_comp$Q3.10), THD_dgn, na.rm=TRUE)  #81% awareness, weighted

aware_xt <- svytable(~EHF_aware_list + EHF_aware_simp, THD_comp, round=T)
aware_know_xt <- svytable(~EHF_aware_list + HF_know, THD_comp, round=T)
aware_donate_xt <- svytable(~EHF_aware_list + HF_donate, THD_comp, round=T)

```

From the Home Depot sample, I estimate that `r round(100*aware_tab$aware.prop.l,0)`% (se = `r round(100*aware_tab$aware.prop.l_se,0)`%) identified emergency cash grants as a job amenity--substantially higher than the 14% of general retail workers who knew Home Depot had an EHF, but still indicating two in five workers remain unaware despite active promotion. Regarding engagement, a remarkable `r round(100*aware_tab$donated.prop)`% (se = `r round(100*aware_tab$donated.prop_se)`%) reported having donated, although 30% of those claiming donation failed to identify emergency cash grants as an amenity, suggesting some respondents may fail to connect the charitable and mutual aid functions of the EHF program. Fifty-four percent report personally knowing a coworker who received a grant. Respectively, `r round(100*aware_tab$applied.prop)`% and  `r round(100*aware_tab$received.prop)`% applied for and received EHF grants. Among workers who reported qualifying hardships in the past year (`r round(100*aware_tab$eligible.prop)`% of sample), `r round(100*takeup$takeup.prop)`% applied to the Homer Fund.^[In Study 2, the applied and "know someone" questions were asked only of treatment group respondents (post-treatment) while the EHF donation and grant receipt questions were asked of all respondents (post treatment).  This differs somewhat from Study 3 (see subsequent footnote).  Nevertheless rates of grant donation and receipt were nearly identical for treated and control respondents, so I include all available observations in Table \@ref(tab:tab-awareness-model).]

```{r ACNT-aware-calcs, echo=FALSE}
aware_tab_wmt<-summarise(wmt.hq_wgt_f,

         received.prop = survey_mean(ehf_received_all=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         donated.prop = survey_mean(ehf_donation=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         eligible.prop = survey_mean(emergency=="Yes", na.rm=T),
         tenure.sd = survey_sd(tenure_num, na.rm=T)
          )
takeup_wmt <- wmt.hq_wgt_f |> 
  filter(ehf_exist != "No", treatment_bin == FALSE, emergency == "Yes") |> 
  summarize(takeup.prop = survey_mean(ehf_applied == "Yes"))

cntlaware_wmt <- wmt.hq_wgt_f |> 
  filter(treatment_bin == FALSE) |> 
  summarize(aware.prop.direct.cntrl = survey_mean(ehf_exist == "Yes"))

aware_wmt_xt <- svytable(~ehf_aware_pretr + ehf_exist, wmt_wgt_f, round=T)
aware_know_wmt_xt <- svytable(~ehf_aware_pretr + ehf_other_recip, wmt_wgt_f, round=T)
aware_donate_wmt_xt <- svytable(~ehf_aware_pretr + ehf_donation, wmt_wgt_f, round=T)

aware_wmt_xt <- svytable(~ehf_aware_pretr + ehf_exist, wmt_wgt_f, round=T)


wmt_cntrl_wgt <- subset(wmt_wgt_f, treatment_bin == FALSE)
aware_wmt_cntrl_xt <- svytable(~ehf_aware_pretr + ehf_exist, wmt_cntrl_wgt, round=T)
```


```{r eval=TRUE, echo = FALSE}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'THD', '3_awareness_models.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)

```

At Walmart  `r round(100*aware_tab_wmt$aware.prop)`% (se = `r round(100*aware_tab_wmt$aware.prop_se)`%) were aware of the ACNT, higher than the 20% of general retail workers identifying an EHF at Walmart but substantially lower than at Home Depot.  Just `r round(100*aware_tab_wmt$know.prop)`% (se = `r round(100*aware_tab_wmt$know.prop_se)`%) claim to know a grant recipient and `r round(100*aware_tab_wmt$donated.prop)`% (se = `r round(100*aware_tab_wmt$donated.prop_se)`%)  claim to have donated. Of those who both knew about the ACNT and experienced a likely qualifying event, `r round(100*takeup_wmt$takeup.prop)`% applied for a grant, 60% of the Home Depot rate.^[Study 3 differed from Study 2 in that I asked all Walmart respondents (not just control respondents) whether their employer has an EHF (post-treatment).  Those incorrectly answering "No" were not shown the EHF engagement questions, reflected in the $N$ in Table \@ref(tab:tab-awareness-model-wmt).  Thus the subset of respondents reporting EHF engagement differs somewhat between Studies 2 and 3.  Nevertheless, restricting the Study 2 sample to only treated respondents produces nearly identical comparisons across studies.]

These awareness gaps reflect differences in program promotion and generosity. More importantly for interpreting experiments, pre-exposed workers differ systematically from the unaware. Tables \@ref(tab:tab-awareness-model) and \@ref(tab:tab-awareness-model-wmt) display results from weighted logistic regressions on EHF awareness and engagement.  Job tenure is the strongest predictor of awareness and engagement across both firms. A one-standard-deviation increase in tenure is associated with a `r round(100*mfx_aware_thd$estimate[2]*aware_tab$tenure.sd)`pp increase in awareness probability at Home Depot and a `r round(100*mfx_aware_wmt$estimate[2]*aware_tab_wmt$tenure.sd)`pp increase at Walmart. Men are significantly less aware and engaged at both firms, consistent with prior CSR research [@brammerContributionCorporateSocial2007a]. Other demographics (race, gender, education, hourly status) show inconsistent relationships across firms and outcomes.

Workers entering the experiment previously exposed to their employer's EHF ("aware") differ systematically from the unaware, especially in job tenure. The survey experiments test whether a one-time exposure to an EHF message shifts attitudes, not how gradual, organic awareness shapes attachment over time or how the introduction of a new program might work. I therefore examine treatment effect heterogeneity by pre-exposure status.^[Note that this was not pre-registered for the Home Depot analysis but core findings were; see Appendix \@ref(app-PAP) for more discussion.]
