## Experimental design

In both studies, I randomly assigned respondents to receive either information about their employer's EHF or to control conditions receiving no EHF information. The core design is similar across studies, with some refinements in Study 3.

The experiment in Study 2 (Home Depot) included three conditions:

* Control ($N=164$): No information about Homer Fund
* _Text_ treatment ($N=197$): Brief, neutral textual description of Homer Fund
* _Video_ treatment ($N=154$): Actual Home Depot-produced promotional video

The text treatment stated: 

> "Your employer, The Home Depot, maintains a program called the Homer Fund. The Homer Fund combines donations from workers like you with money from the Home Depot corporation. The Homer Fund uses this money to offer cash grants of up to $10,000 to Home Depot employees in times of unexpected financial hardship like a natural disaster, illness, or death in the family."

Neutral textual descriptions do not reflect how employers actually communicate with their employees.  As a more realistic intervention, respondents in the video treatment watched a Home Depot-produced testimonial video featuring a Home Depot employee who received Homer Fund assistance during a serious illness.  The video emphasizes emotional themes of family crisis and coworker support.  Figure \@ref(fig:fig-ray), panel (a) displays a still image.^[The video is publicly visible here: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qF-HBoySMe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qF-HBoySMe) and here: [https://corporate.homedepot.com/news/foundation-and-community/homer-fund-celebrates-20-years-giving-rays-story](https://corporate.homedepot.com/news/foundation-and-community/homer-fund-celebrates-20-years-giving-rays-story). The video runs 2:41.]

```{r fig-ray, echo=FALSE, fig.cap = "Screen stills of the video treatments", fig.subcap = c("Home Depot", "Walmart"), out.width="50%", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics( c(
  here('4_output', 'plots','RaysStory.jpeg' ),
  here('4_output', 'plots','Rays_story_wmt.png')
  )
)
```

The Study 3 (Walmart) experiment also included three conditions:

 * Pure control ($N=260$): No information
 * Placebo ($N=254$): Video about Walmart's acquisition of Vizio
 * Video treatment ($N=466$): Adapted EHF video

Note that Study 3 concentrates on a video vignette treatment for the Walmart sample, omitting the text treatment, based on results from the Study 2. Because Walmart does not produce promotional videos for the ACNT and for close comparability to the Home Depot experiment, I produced my own video message that mirrors the Homer Fund video's structure, script, and production style. I hired an actor matching Ray's demographics (white male, approximately age 50) and adapted the script to Walmart/ACNT context. The Walmart video is 41 seconds shorter (trimming only visual transitions, not spoken content). Figure \@ref(fig:fig-ray), panel (b) displays a still image from the beginning of the video.^[Videos can be seen here: [placebo video](https://tinyurl.com/EHF-Study3-placebo); [treatment (solidarity card)](https://tinyurl.com/EHFStudy3-solidarity); [treatment (charity card)](https://tinyurl.com/EHF-Study3-charity).]   

Respondents were randomly divided between treatment and control. To address concerns that effects might reflect generic video exposure rather than EHF content, I added a placebo condition in Study 3. Control respondents were randomized to either receive no video (pure control) or watch a placebo video with identical production values but unrelated content (Walmart's acquisition of Vizio). 

Manipulation checks (see Appendix \@ref(app-manip-wmt)) confirm that the video treatment did indeed increase respondent awareness of the ACNT, as expected whereas the placebo had no effect. Similarly, the ACNT video successfully increased respondents' behavioral willingness to donate to the EHF, as expected, whereas the placebo had no effect (see Appendix \@ref(app-donate-wmt)). I therefore combine the pure and placebo controls in analysis below.^[Within the Study 3 treatment arm, I also randomized between two variations of the video (different title card before pressing play, all other content identical): "charity" framing emphasizing charitable donations vs. "solidarity" framing emphasizing supporting fellow Walmart workers. This pre-registered sub-experiment tested whether solidarity vs. charity framing matters. I found no detectable differences for any outcome (Appendix \@ref(app-framing)), so I pool all treated respondents in the main text.]

Immediately after the experimental condition, all respondents answered questions measuring three key outcomes: financial security, job attachment, and union support. 

## Analytic approach

The main quantities of interest are the average treatment effects (ATE) for each of the EHF treatments relative to control for each of the outcome variables. A key design challenge is that significant proportions of respondents in both studies were already aware of their employer's EHF before the survey.  I therefore examine treatment effect heterogeneity by pre-exposure status.^[Pre-exposure can also be viewed through the lens of compliance with treatment assignment; the pre-exposed are "always takers" while the unexposed are "compliers".  Since I have direct measures of pre-exposure, however, the heterogeneous effects approach is more natural.] 

Pre-exposure to EHF information is not randomly assigned, but it is not a quantity of causal interest.  Rather pre-exposure is a trait that may moderate experimental treatment effects.  The assumption needed to sustain a causal interpretation of experiment treatment is that pre-exposure to information about the EHF is independent of potential outcomes, conditional on treatment and relevant covariates. This is plausible given pre-exposure primarily reflects job tenure (which I condition on) and the list-based awareness measure precedes treatment.  Even this method of measuring awareness before treatment could prime respondents, but three facts suggest this is not a serious concern: the measurement is subtle (embedded in a benefits list), pre-exposed and unexposed workers differ systematically in outcomes and treatment effects, and any priming would bias results toward zero. However, I cannot definitively rule out that pre-exposed and unexposed workers differ on unobserved characteristics that independently predict both awareness and key outcomes.

I produce regression-based estimates of causal effects using OLS with robust standard errors for financial security and job attachment and multinomial logistic regression for the trichotomous union vote. I report three models for each outcome: one that includes only the experimental treatment indicators, providing ATE estimates; one that adds a treatment-by-awareness interaction term; and a third that also includes a suite of pre-registered pre-treatment covariates, including predictors of awareness.^[Full reporting of the coefficient estimates appears in the appendices]  The latter two specifications admit assessments of effect heterogeneity. 

## Results: Study 2 (Home Depot)
### Financial security

Recall that H1 predicts EHF information should improve workers' sense of financial security. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-finsec) displays the distribution of responses by treatment condition;  vertical lines represent 95% confidence intervals.  Just under 40% of Home Depot respondents expressed concern about their ability to meet this financial challenge, in line with recent estimates [@boardofgovernorsofthefederalreservesystemEconomicWellBeingHouseholds2023].^[In Study 1, 31% of respondents reported trouble covering this expense] EHF information does not affect financial security perceptions. If anything, the video treatment produces slightly more pessimism, but effects are not statistically distinguishable from zero.

```{r fig-finsec, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Subjective financial security by treatment status for the Home Depot sample", out.width="70%", fig.align='center'}

temp<-here::here('2_code', 'THD', '4_insecurity_summary_plots.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)
p.ord
```

 Table \@ref(tab:tab-finsec) confirms this null finding across all specifications. Neither text nor video treatment shifts financial security perceptions. Interestingly, workers pre-exposed to the Homer Fund report higher levels of financial security by about 0.5 standard deviations, or half the average distance between outcome categories, even after controlling for tenure and other predictors of awareness. This correlation could reflect the Homer Fund improving security, but absent experimental effects, the relationship is likely spurious (e.g., more financially secure workers stay employed at Home Depot longer or pay more attention to benefits information).  I also examined an alternative measure---self-reported difficulty paying monthly bills---and found identical null results (Appendix \@ref(app-bills)).  Across both measures, exposing Home Depot workers to Homer Fund information does not shift their subjective financial security. H1 is not supported.

```{r tab-finsec, echo=FALSE, tab.cap="OLS regression estimates of treatment effects on subjective financial security at Home Depot."}

temp<-here::here('2_code', 'THD', 'insecurity_models.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)
model_print_uw

```

### Job attachment

Table \@ref(tab:tab-aithd-models) presents OLS regression estimates of treatment effects on the job attachment index.  On average, the text treatment had no detectable effect, but the video treatment increased average job attachment by 0.28 on the index scale, or about 27% of a control group standard deviation.  I also uncover important heterogeneity by pre-exposure status.  Those pre-exposed to the EHF were significantly more positive about their Home Depot job than the unexposed by about 60% of a standard deviation, even accounting for predictors of EHF awareness. 

```{r tab-aithd-models, echo=FALSE, tab.cap="OLS regression estimates of treatment effects on job attachment at Home Depot."}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'THD', '6_loyalty_models.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)
model_print_thd_uw_attachment
```

In contrast to findings for financial security, I recover positive and significant treatment effects for job attachment. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-THD-effattach) displays predicted outcomes by treatment and pre-exposure status (derived from the covariate model), revealing important heterogeneity. Among workers who were unaware of the Homer Fund before the survey, the video treatment produces a large positive effect (approximately 40% of an SD). Among workers already aware of the Homer Fund, treatment effects vanish; exposure to additional information does not further increase attachment. This pattern is theoretically sensible: emotional messages affect those learning something new more than those already informed.

```{r fig-attachment-plot-thd, eval = FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Treatment effects on job attachment", out.width="70%", fig.align='center'}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'THD', '5_loyalty_summary_plots.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)
p.ai_thd
```

```{r fig-THD-effattach, echo=FALSE, fig.cap = "Interpreting treatment effects on Home Depot job attachment by EHF pre-exposure status", out.width="70%", fig.align='center'}
THDattach_eff_plot
```

Examining individual components of the attachment index (Appendix \@ref(app-cov) and \@ref(app-full-wmt)), I find consistent positive effects of the video treatment across loyalty to coworkers, loyalty to employer, and willingness to recommend, although the employer loyalty effect is smaller and marginally significant.

For Home Depot, H3 is supported: EHF messages increase job attachment, particularly among previously unaware workers. The effect size is substantively meaningful. This occurs despite no improvement in financial security, suggesting the mechanism is symbolic or affective rather than material.

### Support for unionization {#sec-hd-union-support}

```{r wern-eval, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'wern_supplemental.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-uv-thd) shows union vote intentions by treatment condition. Home Depot workers are generally skeptical of unions: only `r round(100*summary_tab_c$prounion)`% (se =  `r round(100*summary_tab_c$prounion_se)`% )  of control respondents reporting a willingness to vote for a union and `r round(100*summary_tab_c$antiunion,2)`% (se =   `r round(100*summary_tab_c$antiunion_se,2)`% ) voting against (the remainder answered "not sure").  This is substantially more anti-union than retail workers generally (Study 1 found `r round(100*genpop_engage_sum$union_support)`% would vote for a union) or even Walmart workers (see below).^[In the summer 2022 survey from @ahlquist2022WERNWorkers2025,  `r round(100*wern_uv_dist$prop[1])`% (se= `r round(100*wern_uv_dist$prop_se[1])`%) of front-line retail workers reported a willingness to vote for unionization.  Home Depot workers were already less interested in unionization relative to the industry average.] 

```{r fig-uv-thd,eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Support for unionization by treatment status in the Home Depot sample", out.width="70%", fig.align='center'}

temp<-here::here('2_code', 'THD', '7_uiuv_summary_plots.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)
uv_plot
```

The video treatment clearly shifts responses away from "for the union" toward "not sure", but not toward greater opposition. The text treatment shows similar but weaker patterns.  On average, the video treatment makes respondents more _uncertain_ about their support for unionization. Answering the question rather than skipping it suggests that this pattern is not the result of disinterest or satisficing.

Table \@ref(tab:tab-uv) reports multinomial logistic regression results.  The base model shows that video treatment, on average, produces an increase in the "not sure" responses, echoing Figure \@ref(fig:fig-uv-thd).  Once I account for pre-exposure, a clearer pattern emerges. Those aware of the EHF prior to the experiment were _already_ significantly less supportive of unions than the unexposed. Among workers unaware of the Homer Fund, both treatments significantly reduce pro-union responses, with larger effects for the video condition.  Including covariates predictive of pre-exposure does not alter conclusions.    

```{r tab-uv, eval=TRUE, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, tab.cap="Multinomial logit regression models on support for unionization "}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'THD', '8_uv_models.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)

multinom_tab

```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-uveff) translates these logit coefficients into predicted probabilities by pre-exposure status. Among the previously unaware (left column), the video treatment more than halves predicted union support from about `r round(100*eff_probs$prob[1,"prob.For.the.union"])`% to `r round(100*eff_probs$prob[3,"prob.For.the.union"])`%. This effect does not come from increasing active opposition but rather from making workers uncertain. The proportion answering "not sure" grows from  `r round(100*eff_probs$prob[1,"prob.Not.sure"])`% to almost `r round(100*eff_probs$prob[3,"prob.Not.sure"])`%.

Among workers already aware of the Homer Fund (right column), treatment effects differ. The pre-exposed are already less supportive of unions on average, and additional exposure to Homer Fund messaging does not further reduce this low support.  But it does increase uncertainty from `r round(100*eff_probs$prob[4,"prob.Not.sure"])`% to almost `r round(100*eff_probs$prob[6,"prob.Not.sure"])`%

```{r fig-uveff, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.height=8, fig.cap="Interpreting heterogeneous treatment effects on union support (Home Depot sample)", out.width="70%", fig.align='center'}
#dev.new(width = 6000, height = 1500, unit = "px")
print(mnl_eff_plot)

```

H4 is supported at Home Depot: EHF information reduces support for unionization but not by converting pro-union workers to anti-union positions. Instead, exposure to EHF messaging increases ambivalence. The message may raise doubts about what unions would add or signal employer responsiveness that makes unions seem less necessary.  This effect's visiblilty alongside an increase in job attachment and in the absence of any effect on financial security is consistent with @bladerWhatLeadsOrganizational2007's finding that perceived employer fairness and identification with co-workers affect union support independent of economic considerations.   The concentration of effects among previously unaware workers is again theoretically sensible but has important implications: the Homer Fund may be most effective at shaping attitudes of workers who haven't yet developed strong attachments or opinions.

## Results: Study 3 (Walmart)

I follow an identical analytic approach with Study 3's Walmart workers.

### Financial security

```{r}
ee.prop<-summarise(wmt.hq_wgt_f, 
          survey_mean(emergency_expense_num >0.5))
```

Walmart workers are notably more financially precarious than Home Depot workers, with `r round(100*(1-ee.prop$coef))`% expressing concern about their ability to meet a \$400 emergency expense, 25 percentage points higher than among Home Depot workers.  This aligns with other indicators: in the samples, 35% of Walmart respondents reported accessing government welfare programs in the past year versus 20% at Home Depot.

Table \@ref(tab:tab-finsec-wmt) displays OLS regression-based estimates of treatment effects on financial security. As at Home Depot, there are no detectable effects. Pre-exposed respondents report greater financial resilience (0.1 scale points or 27% of a control group standard deviation), but treatment does not shift beliefs among either aware or unaware workers.

```{r tab-finsec-wmt, eval=TRUE, echo = FALSE, tab.cap="Financial Security (Walmart)"}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'Walmart', '7_attachment_summary_plots_WMT.R')
source(temp)

temp<-here::here('2_code', 'Walmart', '10_insecurity_models_WMT.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)

model_print_sec_wmt

#temp<-here::here('2_code', 'Walmart', '7_attachment_summary_plots_WMT.R')
#source(temp)
#rm(temp)
```

H1 remains unsupported. Across both firms, intensive, realistic EHF messages do not improve subjective financial security--the programs' stated purpose.

### Job attachment

In addition to feeling more financially precarious, Walmart respondents express lower baseline job attachment than Home Depot workers.  For example, the net promoter score among the Walmart control respondents was `r round(100*nps[[1]],2)`%, seven percentage points lower than at Home Depot.^[Net promoter score is % promoters - % detractors for the recommend employer question, a common indicator of aggregate support.]  This suggests that Walmart workers are coming in to the survey with a more negative set of experiences and expectations about their employer than the Home Depot sample, consistent with the description of corporate culture from @sullMeasuringCultureLeading2019.  

Table \@ref(tab:tab-attachment-models-wmt) presents treatment effects on the attachment index. These models again show that those pre-exposed to the EHF are more attached to their jobs, even after conditioning on predictors of EHF awareness. But the ACNT video treatment produces a small effect on job attachment that is indistinguishable from zero. Effects do not vary by pre-exposure.

```{r tab-attachment-models-wmt, eval=TRUE, echo = FALSE, tab.cap="Job attachment (Walmart)"}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'Walmart', '8_attachment_models_WMT.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)

model_print_attachment_hq
```

Examining individual components (Appendix \@ref(app-full-wmt)) shows similar null results across loyalty to coworkers, loyalty to employer, willingness to recommend, and quit intentions. The ACNT message simply does not move these attitudes.  H3 is not supported at Walmart. 

Importantly, the null finding is not a failed replication; manipulation checks indicate the experiment worked as intended.  The contrast with results among Home Depot workers could be due to (1) the ACNT is just not generous enough to be meaningful to workers; (2) less aggressive employer promotion makes the adapted video seem disingenuous, or (3) workers perceive inconsistency between ACNT messaging and their broader experiences at Walmart. Although I cannot distinguish among these possibilities in this study, they all connect with the idea that EHFs are part of a bundle of workplace practices.

### Support for unionization

Walmart workers are substantially more pro-union than Home Depot workers: 44% of control respondents would vote for a union versus 25% at Home Depot. Only 18% actively oppose unions.

Table \@ref(tab:tab-uv-models-wmt) displays results for a multinomial logistic regression on willingness to vote for unionization. The ACNT video produces a significant decrease in opposition to unions. Adding pre-exposure generates notably worse-fitting models while still producing a negative but less precisely estimated effect on anti-union vote intentions.^[Appendix \@ref(app-full-wmt) displays full covariate estimates for both the model with covariates but no pre-exposure terms and the "covariate" model reported in Table \@ref(tab:tab-uv-models-wmt).  The model excluding pre-exposure terms is the better fitting based on the AIC and BIC.  In this preferred model, the estimated treatment effect and standard error are quite close to the base model in Table \@ref(tab:tab-uv-models-wmt).]   

```{r tab-uv-models-wmt, eval=TRUE, echo = FALSE, tab.cap="Support for unionization (Walmart)"}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'Walmart', '12_uv_models_WMT.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)
multinom_tab_wmt
```

I use the base model to generate predicted probabilities. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-uv-models-wmt) displays the estimated _difference_ between treatment and control in the predicted probability of choosing each outcome category.  On average, the ACNT treatment video lowered the probability of voting against the union from about 21% to 16%. The probability of voting "for the union" increases from 43% to 47%, absorbing most of the shift. The "not sure" category changes minimally. 

```{r fig-uv-models-wmt, eval=TRUE, echo = FALSE, fig.cap="Difference in predicted probability between treated and control (treatment effect) on support for unionization with 95% confidence intervals (Walmart)", out.width="70%", fig.align='center', fig.pos='H'}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'Walmart', '12_uv_models_WMT.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)
wmt_mnl_uv_interp
```

The effect on expected union support among co-workers tells a similar story. Table \@ref(tab:tab-usupp-models-wmt) shows the ACNT video increases Walmart workers' estimates of the proportion of their coworkers voting for a union by about 4 percentage points on a baseline of 50%. This suggests the video makes workers perceive unionization as more viable or acceptable among their peers.

```{r tab-usupp-models-wmt, eval=TRUE, echo = FALSE, tab.cap="Treatment effects on expected union support among co-workers"}
union_supp_pct_tab_wmt
```

These findings contradict H4 and differ from what we observed at Home Depot. At Walmart, EHF messages reduce _opposition_ to unions rather than reducing support.

    n                 = unweighted(n()),
    delay_median      = survey_median(HF_delay_num,           na.rm = TRUE),
    delay_week_or_less = survey_mean(HF_delay_week_or_less, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

wmt_delay <- wmt_recipients |>
  summarise(
    n                  = unweighted(n()),
    delay_median       = survey_median(ehf_delay_num,              na.rm = TRUE),
    delay_week_or_less = survey_mean(ehf_delay_week_or_less,   na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# ── Followup among recipients ─────────────────────────────────────────────

thd_followup <- thd_recipients |>
  summarise(
    n        = unweighted(n()),
    followup = survey_mean(HF_followup, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

wmt_followup <- wmt_recipients |>
  summarise(
    n        = unweighted(n()),
    followup = survey_mean(ehf_followup_bin, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

```

At both firms, exposure to realistic EHF messages fails to improve perceived financial security (H1 rejected). Yet at Home Depot, the same message significantly increased job attachment and reduced union support by increasing ambivalence among previously unaware workers (H3, H4 supported). Effects are stronger for video than textual treatments, indicating that a multimedia message with an emotional narrative elicits stronger reactions than a text-based factual description.  At Walmart the pattern reverses. An identically-delivered ACNT message produces no attachment gains and reduces opposition to unionization (H3, H4 contradicted). What explains these divergent findings?

One possible explanation is the three-year gap between Study 2 (Fall 2021) and Study 3 (Fall 2024). During the intervening period, there were several high-profile unionization campaigns that may have shifted attitudes toward unions and employers, including how workers respond to the EHF messages.  With the data available, I am unable to completely rule out this possiblity.  Nevertheless, this explanation is not totally satisfying. Union support was rising nationally since before the coronavirus pandemic [@ahlquistRiseUnionCurious2024; @sojournerAmericansFavorLabor2025]. The period of broad opinion change around unions was well underway by the time of the Home Depot survey.  The key quantities are within-study treatment effects (induced changes), not cross-study comparisons in average outcome levels. Walmart workers in the 2024 sample are  more pro-union at baseline, which could reflect either temporal trends or persistent firm  differences.  In Section \@ref(sec-hd-union-support), I presented evidence that in 2021-22 Home Depot was already a firm with low levels of union support relative to the retail industry, whereas Walmart workers' attitudes are about average. 

If secular pro-union trends changed how workers interpret private welfare programs, then we would expect a stronger correlation between EHF awareness and support for unionization unions in 2025 compared to 2021-22.  Available survey evidence suggests this did _not_ happen.  In the 2025 survey from Study 1, there was no relationship between EHF awareness and pro-union vote intentions among a sample of retail workers (see Appendix \@ref(app-genpop-est)). A separate 2022 survey of front-line retail workers also included a plausible indicator of EHF awareness [@ahlquist2022WERNWorkers2025].  In Appendix \@ref(app-wern) I show that this survey produces a similar (lack of) correlation between EHF awareness and union voting intentions. The cross-sectional relationship between EHF awareness and union vote intention is stable across two independent surveys three years apart, despite a documented national rise in union sentiment during that period. This suggests any temporal confound was not sufficiently large to move this relationship on an industry-wide basis.  If EHF effects depend on program characteristics, averaging across firms with different programs may well produce a null average relationship, even as there may be within firm effects. 

The divergent findings between Home Depot and Walmart are consistent with H5, which draws on the perceived organizational support literature [@eisenbergerPerceivedOrganizationalSupport2020]. Workers attribute coherent intentions and values to their employers. They see EHFs as signals about their  employers' intentions, but programs are not interpreted in isolation.  They are calibrated in the context of a bundle of observable practices and a history of experiences [@baronConsistentHumanResource1999]. Whether an EHF message generates loyalty then depends on whether workers find it credible, i.e., consistent with what they already know about how their employer treats them, and adequate to the scale of the problem that the program's existence acknowledges.

Home Depot workers encounter the Homer Fund in a workplace with active EHF outreach through social media, donation drives, and integration into corporate ESG reporting. The program is relatively generous and accessible. Walmart workers are less likely to be aware of the ACNT, given weaker promotion. Those who are aware experience a less-generous ACNT in a cost-control culture [@sullMeasuringCultureLeading2019; @wartzmanStillBrokeWalmarts2022].

In Studies 2 and 3, grant recipients' experiences reflect these differences in implementation. Among Walmart respondents who reported receiving a grant, only `r round(100 * wmt_coverage$cov_half_plus)`% said  the grant covered at least half of their emergency need, compared with  `r round(100 * thd_coverage$cov_half_plus)`% at Home Depot. When asked whether anyone from  the employer followed up afterward, `r round(100 * wmt_followup$followup)`% of Walmart  recipients said yes, compared to `r round(100 * thd_followup$followup)`% at Home Depot.^[EHFs were similar in payout speed; `r round(100 * thd_delay$delay_week_or_less)`% and `r round(100 * wmt_delay$delay_week_or_less)`% of grantees at Home Depot and Walmart, respectively, received funds within seven days of approval.]

Under this interpretation, the Homer Fund message increases attachment and reduces union support among previously unaware Home Depot workers because it resonates with other workplace experiences and it is adequate to the needs it claims to address. The ACNT message produces no attachment gains and reduces opposition to unions among Walmart workers because it may ring hollow, drawing attention to the gap between what the employer acknowledges workers need and what it actually provides.

This interpretation is plausible but the present studies cannot confirm it. Neither Study 2 nor Study 3 directly measured workers' assessments of program credibility or consistency with organizational culture.  Survey length precluded the inclusion of complete, validated  organizational support scales. The two firms also differ on dimensions beyond their EHF programs such as product mix and  workforce composition.  With two cases I cannot isolate which features drive the difference. Further research that directly measures worker perceptions of program credibility across a larger set of firms with varying program characteristics will be needed.  But at a descriptive level, the divergent findings suggest that EHFs are not universally effective loyalty-builders; their effects are connected to the broader employment context.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This paper documents Employee Hardship Funds, a widespread but unstudied organizational practice that blends welfare capitalism, worker mutual aid, and CSR.  I provide the first systematic evidence on worker knowledge and attitudes around these programs.

Three findings stand out. First, retail workers value the idea of a rapid-response emergency fund, on par with improved health insurance, suggesting a real need.  Nevertheless, awareness is modest. Only 23% of retail workers report that their employer offers emergency cash assistance.  At Walmart, the majority of workers were unaware of this amenity. Why does a benefit workers value remain so invisible? Possible mechanisms include short retention or optimism bias among workers and insufficient outreach by employers.

Second, workers respond to realistic EHF messages in ways that increase attachment and shift union attitudes even when those messages produce no detectable improvement in their immediate sense of financial security.  This suggests that the process producing these effects is not simply the material reassurance these programs claim to provide. 

Third, EHF effects are contingent. Messages about Home Depot's generous, heavily promoted, and culturally integrated EHF produced the expected governance effects. Walmart's less generous program in a cost-control culture produced no attachment gains and reduced opposition to unions--the opposite of presumed employer interests. With two firms I cannot isolate the features that drive differences, but the contrast is consistent with arguments that complementarity across HR and governance practices matter.  Private welfare programs like EHFs are most usefully understood as part of a larger bundle of employment practices, not an isolated intervention. Workers evaluate them accordingly. 

For labor relations researchers and practitioners, this paper offers the first evidence on a mechanism that the welfare capitalism literature has long hypothesized but rarely tested experimentally: that employer-provided benefits can substitute for collective voice by shifting workers' felt relationship with their employer. At Home Depot, a generous and culturally integrated EHF does precisely what union substitution theories predict: reduce pro-union sentiment. But this happens through increased ambivalence rather than opposition. Workers do not become more hostile to unions; they become uncertain whether unions are necessary. The Walmart finding is equally instructive: when the same logic is applied through an inadequate program, it reverses. Rather than substituting for collective voice, a plausibly insufficient welfare gesture can highlight the gap between what workers need and what their employer provides, making unionization seem more rather than less attractive. At the margin, inadequate employer welfare programs may enhance rather than threaten organizing opportunities.

For managers, a well-designed and promoted EHF can strengthen employee attachment, but token programs risk highlighting inadequacy rather than demonstrating support.  To address this risk, managers should consider an EHF in the context of a broader HR practices.  A new EHF (or an outreach drive) may work well if introduced after wage increases or demonstrated improvement in scheduling practices. A bolt-on program in the context of low morale is unlikely to yield benefits. An EHF of sufficient scale and generosity to be meaningful combined with sustained, multi-channel promotion are minimal ingredients for success.  Once implemented, an ongoing challenge is striking the right balance between verifying actual emergencies and rapid delivery of urgently needed funds.  More worker involvement in EHF design and operation could help in this regard, enhancing the program's perceived consistency and adequacy among those workers.

For policymakers, EHFs illustrate that private welfare can supplement but not substitute for robust public social insurance. They also highlight how existing public safety net programs are cumbersome and often fail to deliver during acute need. The EHFs studied here function as governance tools while delivering modest, discretionary aid. EHFs are government-subsidized programs, benefiting from tax-deductible donations and tax-exempt grants. It is unclear whether they are cost-effective safety-net supplements or symptoms of an inadequate public system.  Currently there are no minimum standards for program generosity, accessibility, coverage, or reporting required to secure and maintain these tax advantages.

## Limitations and future research {#sec-limitations}

This study has several important limitations. First, although the video treatments mirrored real-world messages from employers, one-time exposure in a survey is not the sustained, multi-channel promotion through which workers may naturally encounter EHF information. The findings here demonstrate that EHF messages can shift attitudes; whether such effects accumulate, decay, or interact with repeated real-world exposure remains unknown. The concentration of effects among previously unaware workers suggests that initial exposure may be particularly impactful. I cannot speak to how attitudes evolve with ongoing engagement.

Second, and related, I measure only short-term attitudes and intentions, not long-term behavior.  I attempted a pre-registered one-week follow-up survey in Study 3 to assess effect persistence but achieved only a 16% response rate ($N=157$), leaving the study underpowered. I detected no significant effects at follow-up, but cannot distinguish between genuine effect decay and inadequate statistical power; see Appendix \@ref(app-followup-wmt).  

Third, reliance on social media recruitment likely excludes workers with limited internet access and those less engaged with social media, possibly the most precarious workers for whom EHFs might matter most. The older average age in the samples (47 years) compared to the retail workforce suggests selection toward more stable, longer-tenured workers. Effects among younger, more transient workers may differ.

Fourth, with only two firms, I observe that effects vary across organizational contexts, but cannot pinpoint the full causal process. To make progress addressing all these limitations, future research will need to track workers longitudinally, exploit variation in EHF adoption timing, examine behavioral outcomes, and study more firms in more industries that vary in program characteristics, all difficult tasks.

# More Background on EHFs and EHF third party providers {#app-3rd}

In 2001, the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) amended its rules to allow employer-controlled non-profit foundations to provide direct cash assistance to employees who under certain conditions, called a "qualifying event". Funds can only be used for basic living expenses (food, clothing, transportation, housing/house repair, burial) for the recipient and immediate family [@internalrevenueserviceDisasterReliefProviding2014; @aprillCharitableClassDisaster2016]. So long as these guidelines are followed, EHFs are tax-exempt charities; donations are tax deductible.  
 
There are now multiple organizations that provide EHF outsourcing services to firms.  Beyond the Employee Assistance Foundation, I have identified E4E Relief, America's Charities, and Canary.  EAF appears to be the largest and claims to have over 400 clients [@employeeassistancefoundationDecadeAssistanceOffering2022]. 
Figure \@ref(fig:fig-tpm) illustrates the scale and growth of EHFs using data from IRS 990 forms.^[If a firm contracts with a third party to administer an EHF program, all donations and grants are linked to the third party contractor's EIN, not the original firm.  With a large number of employers offering EHFs through third party providers, I cannot systematically identify firms with and without EHFs through IRS 990 filings.] Figure \@ref(fig:fig-tpm) compares the revenues and total grants paid out to individuals from four EHF outsourcing organizations.  EAF, the oldest and largest, has grown rapidly since first appearing in IRS data in 2012, reaching over \$144 million in revenue and \$86 million in grants to individuals in 2020. The data also show the recent entry of several competitor organizations, with E4E and America's Charities operating a similar scales in recent years and Canary growing rapidly.

# Measurement {#app-measurement}

This appendix provides detailed information on all measures used in Studies 1-3, including item wording, response scales, and psychometric properties.

## Item wording and response scales for key outcome variables

### EHF Awareness (List-based measure) {#app-HFaware}

My preferred "list-based" measure of EHF awareness comes from a question in which respondents were shown a list of eight workplace benefits and programs and asked: *"Employers sometimes create programs or offer benefits for their workers. Which of the benefits on this list are offered to workers like you at [Employer name]? Please select all that apply."*

The list varied slightly by survey:

- Paid sick days
- Paid vacation days
- Health plan or medical insurance  
- A retirement plan other than Social Security
- **Emergency cash assistance to help in unexpected hard times** [Study 1,3]/ **Cash grant to help in times of financial emergency** [Study 2]
- Paid parental leave
- Free or subsidized childcare [Study 1, 3]/Company provided or subsidized childcare [Study 2]
- Tuition discount or reimbursement for schooling [Study 1, 3]
- None of these [Study 2]

**Coding:** Respondents who selected the bolded item were coded as aware of EHF (1 = aware, 0 = not aware).

I used the list-based approach for two main reasons.  First, I wanted to avoid contaminating the experiment by priming respondents pre-treatment, so I embedded the item in a longer list and did not use the program name.  Second, this approach avoids problems with demand effects.   

To provide bounds on awareness, I asked other questions of subsets of the respondents.  In studies 2 & 3, control group respondents saw no information about the EHF in the survey.  One measure of prior EHF awareness is therefore the proportion of control group respondents who answer "yes" to a direct question about whether their employer has an EHF. In Study 2, I asked control group respondents only the following: 

> "Some companies have programs that take donations and provide emergency cash to help workers like you through hard times. Does The Home Depot offer a program like this for workers like you?"  

On this basis, I estimate the weighted proportion of Home Depot control-condition respondents who report knowing about the EHF as `r round(aware_tab$aware.prop.s,2)` (se = `r round(aware_tab$aware.prop.s_se,2)`).  The difference in estimated awareness produced by this measure of awareness and the list approach used in the main text is striking.  Among those in the control group correctly answering "yes" to the direct question about their employer's EHF, `r round(100*aware_xt["FALSE","Yes"]/sum(aware_xt[,"Yes"]),0)`% _failed_ to identify the cash grant program as one of their job benefits whereas nearly all of those correctly choosing the cash grant program from the list of benefits also correctly answered direct question.  Consequently, I interpret the lower estimate based on the "list" question as the more accurate reflection of EHF awareness.  Using the list measure of awareness, I estimate that 58% of the Home Depot sample control condition respondents are aware.  This suggests that the direct questions capture vague awareness, possibly combined with some demand effects, rather than functional understanding of the program.

In Study 3, I refined the question ordering such that I asked all respondents the direct questions about whether Walmart has an EHF.  I was careful to implement this question after the survey experiment and answers to key outcome questions.  As shown in Appendix \@ref(app-manip-wmt), both correctly answering the list-based awareness question and video treatment are strongly predictive of a correct answer in the direct question, as expected.  For comparability to Study 2, in Study 3  among those in the control group correctly answering "yes" to the direct question about their employer's EHF, `r round(100*aware_wmt_xt["FALSE","Yes"]/sum(aware_wmt_xt[,"Yes"]),0)`% _failed_ to identify the cash grant program as one of their job amenities.  Of those recorded as "pre-exposed", `r round(100*sum(aware_wmt_cntrl_xt["TRUE","Yes"])/sum(aware_wmt_cntrl_xt["TRUE",]))`% correctly answered yes to the direct question and `r round(100*sum(aware_wmt_cntrl_xt["TRUE","No"])/sum(aware_wmt_cntrl_xt["TRUE",]))`% incorrectly answered "no", with the balance saying they were not sure (a response option not available to the control respondents in Study 2).


### EHF engagement
The EHF engagement questions were asked of different subsets of the of respondents in Study 2 and 3, based on question ordering and a desire to avoid any contamination of the experiment.

*"Do you know someone personally who has received money from [EHF name]?* 

*"Have you ever applied to the [EHF name] for financial assistance?"* 

*"Have you ever received financial assistance from the [EHF name]?"*

*"Have you ever made a donation to the [EHF name]"*

Response scale:  Yes, No, Don't know

In Study 2, the "know beneficiary" and "applied" questions were only presented to treated respondents.  The donate and grant receipt question were asked of all respondents (post treatment).  In these latter two questions, rates of reported donation and receipt were nearly identical among the treated and control groups.   

Study 3 differed from Study 2 in that I asked all Walmart respondents (not just control respondents) whether their employer has an EHF (post-treatment).  Those incorrectly answering "No" were _not_ shown the EHF engagement questions.  Thus the subset of respondents reporting EHF engagement differs somewhat between Studies 2 and 3.  Nevertheless, restricting the Study 2 sample to only treated respondents produces nearly identical quantities to those reported in the main text.  

### Financial Security

*"How confident are you that you could come up with $400 if an unexpected need arose within the next month?"*

Response scale:

1. I am certain I could not come up with \$400
2. I could probably not come up with \$400
3. I could probably come up with \$400
4. I am certain I could come up with the full \$400

This item is taken from the Federal Reserve Board's Survey of Household Economics and Decision-making (SHED), where it has been used since 2013 to track financial fragility [@groverWhat400Emergency2021]. The \$400 threshold reflects realistic emergency expenses for low-wage workers and has become a standard benchmark in research on financial precarity.  This particular item correlates strongly with self-reported financial indicators such as bank account balances, debt levels, and employment shocks [@boardofgovernorsofthefederalreservesystemEconomicWellBeingHouseholds2023]. 


### Loyalty to coworkers and employer

*"How much loyalty would you say you feel toward other workers at [Employer]?"*

*"How much loyalty would you say you feel toward [Employer] as a company?"*

Response scale:

1. No loyalty at all
2. Only a little loyalty
3. Some loyalty
4. A lot of loyalty

Both loyalty questions are taken from @freemanWorkerRepresentationParticipation1998 and analyzed in @freemanSharedCapitalismWork2010.

### Willingness to Recommend Employer

*"If a friend asked you about working at [Employer] doing a job like yours, how likely is it that you would recommend [Employer] as a place to work?"*

Response scale:

1. Definitely would not recommend
2. Might not recommend
3. Not sure
4. Might recommend
5. Certainly would recommend

This item is adapted from the Net Promoter Score (NPS) methodology commonly used in customer and worker satisfaction research.

### Quit Intentions (Study 3 only)

*"Taking everything into consideration, how likely is it you will make a genuine effort to find a new job within the next 3 months?"*

Response scale:

1. Not at all likely
2. Not very likely
3. Somewhat likely
4. Very likely
5. Extremely likely

This item is the core quit intentions question used in the SHIFT Project [@schneiderWhatFacebookTool2019]. Note this item is reverse-scaled relative to other job attachment index questions.

### Union Vote Intention

*"If an election were held today to decide whether employees like you should be represented by a union at [EMPLOYER], would you vote for the union or against the union?"*

Response scale:

- For the union
- Against the union
- Not sure

This is the standard question used in research on support for unionization at work, with a long history in industrial relations research (see @kochanWorkerVoiceAmerica2019, @ahlquistRiseUnionCurious2024, @freemanWhatUnions1984).  Vote intention is a concrete behavioral intention, not an abstract attitude. The question reflects the union certification voting process in the US, giving it strong face validity.

### Expected Coworker Union Support (Study 3 only)

*"If an election were held today to decide whether employees like you should be represented by a union at [Employer], what percent of your co-workers do you think would vote for the union?"*

Response scale: Open numeric response from 0 to 100.

## Job attachment index construction and reliability {#app-attachmentindex}

My goal with the job attachment index is not to argue for a novel psychological concept and propose a measurement scale. Rather I seek to provide a coherent and concise indicator of affective attachment to a particular job, encompassing both horizontal ties to coworkers and vertical ties to the employer.  

There are multiple validated indices purporting to measure "organizational identification", "organizational commitment", "organizational citizenship", and related concepts and subscales [@oreillyOrganizationalCommitmentPsychological1986; @zhaoInfluenceCorporateSocial2022; @mowdayOrganizationalCommitmentQuestionnaire1979; @meyerOrganizationalCommitmentScales1993].  As I had limited survey space, multiple research goals, and limited prior information, I elected not to implement any of these detailed and lengthy instruments designed to measure concepts only loosely connected to the research goals. Instead I focus a few items with strong face validity and history of use in other surveys. 

I constructed a job attachment index from items measuring loyalty to coworkers, loyalty to employer, and willingness to recommend employer. In Study 3, I also included quit intentions (reverse-coded).

### Exploratory Factor Analysis

For both Studies 2 and 3, I conducted exploratory factor analysis on the index components.  In both cases, I use minimum residual factoring methods and the oblimin rotation.  As there are many criteria for selecting factor solutions, I look at the preferred solution across multiple different criteria [@ludeckeExtractingComputingExploring2020].  In both cases, a single factor solution is preferred.

#### Home Depot {#app-HFattachment}

```{r fig-fa-plot-thd, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, out.width = "60%", fig.align='center'}
thd.jai.df<- THD_comp_uw[,c("wrk_loyal_num", "emp_loyal_num", "emp_reco_num")]
nf.thd <- parameters::n_factors(thd.jai.df)
plot(nf.thd)
```

```{r tab-fa-thd, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

fa.thd<-parameters::factor_analysis(thd.jai.df)
fa.thd.tab <- fa.thd |> 
  kable(
  #format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Variable", "Loading", "Complexity", "Uniqueness"),
  caption = "Factor loadings and uniqueness from one-factor solution, Home Depot (study 2)"
)

fa.thd.tab

```

A single factor explains `r round(100*summary(fa.thd)$MR1[2])`% of the variance.  All items load substantively on the first factor (loadings >.60).

#### Walmart {#app-indexcomps-wmt}

```{r fig-fa-plot-wmt, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, out.width = "60%", fig.align='center'}

### Internal consistency \& reliability
```{r tab-alpha-calc, eval=TRUE, results='asis'}
# Study 2
alpha_thd <- psych::alpha(thd.jai.df, check.keys=TRUE)
alpha_value_s2 <- alpha_thd$total$std.alpha
mean_r_s2 <- alpha_thd$total$average_r

# Study 3
alpha_wmt <- psych::alpha(wmt.jai.df, check.keys=TRUE)
alpha_value_s3 <- alpha_wmt$total$std.alpha
mean_r_s3 <- alpha_wmt$total$average_r

reliability_table <- data.frame(
  Sample = c("Study 2 (Home Depot)", "Study 3 (Walmart)"),
  Items = c("3 items", "4 items"),
  N = c(515, 980),
  Alpha = c(alpha_thd$total$std.alpha, alpha_wmt$total$std.alpha),
  Mean_inter_item_r = c(mean_r_s2, mean_r_s3)
)

kable(reliability_table,
      caption = "Cronbach's Alpha for Job Attachment Index",
      col.names = c("Sample", "Items", "N", "alpha", "Mean inter-item r"),
      digits = 2,
      booktabs = TRUE) #%>%
  #kable_styling(
    #latex_options = c("hold_position")
   # )
```

Reliability is good in both samples ($\alpha > .70$) as is inter-item correlations (in the .50 range), supporting the use of a composite index.  The factor structure across the Walmart and Home Depot samples appear quite similar in both loadings and variance explained. Both show a single dominant factor with comparable reliability.  Raw correlations between index items as well as other outcome variables appear in Appendices \@ref(app-survsum-uw) and \@ref(app-wmt-survsum).

# Video treatment and placebo similarities {#app-vidsim}

Here we use text, acoustic, and dynamic video embeddings to describe the multimodal similarties between (i) the placebo and treatment videos for Walmart and (ii) the Home Depot and Walmart treatment videos.  We assessed treatment video comparability using CLIP ViT-B/32 [@radfordLearningTransferableVisual2021], implemented via OpenCLIP on 200 frames per file.  For acoustic similarity, we segmented audio tracks into overlapping 10-second windows and encoded them with CLAP [@wuLargeScaleContrastiveLanguageAudio2023].  For transcript comparability we used Sentence-BERT embeddings [@reimersSentenceBERTSentenceEmbeddings2019] for semantic similarity of the narrated content.  In each case, we report the cosine similarity of the mean embeddings as the video-level similarity score.

Exactly as designed, the placebo and treatment videos display high video similarity and acoustic similarlity but low semantic content similarity. The Home Depot and Walmart treatment videos show very high cosine similarity in video, audio, and semantic content. 

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.cap="Multimodal Similarity: Walmart Treatment vs. Walmart Placebo", fig.align="center"}

## Donation behavior (Walmart) {#app-donate-wmt}

```{r, results = 'asis'}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'Walmart', '14_donate_models_WMT.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)
```

At the end of Study 3, respondents had the opportunity to click on a link to take them to a page where they could donate to the ACNT. Based on past research [@andreoniPowerAskingHow2011], I expect those exposed to the emotional appeal in the video to be more willing to donate.  

In the Walmart sample, I see a low baseline willingness to click on the link of `r round(100*donation_summary$prop[1])`%.  Nevertheless, those seeing the EHF video were about 4 percentage points more likely to take an action to donate. Table \@ref(tab:tab-donate-models-wmt-app) presents regression-based estimates of treatment effects, using OLS and logistic regression.  I also include Firth regression to address concerns with rare events.  Treatment significantly increases willingness to take an action to donate.

# Charity and Solidarity framing experiment effects on union vote and expected co-worker union support (Walmart) {#app-framing}

```{r echo = FALSE, tab.cap = "MNL on union vote, accounting for framing experiment (Walmart)", results= 'asis'}
modelsummary(uv_wmt_mnl_frame,
             gof_map = gm,
             shape = term + response ~ statistic,
             title = "MNL on union vote, accounting for framing experiment (Walmart) \\label{tab:tab-app-mnl-framing-wmt}",
             notes = "Reference category is 'for the union.' Standard errors in parentheses",
             #output = "flextable",
             output = "kableExtra",
             stars = c('$^+$'=.1,'*' = .05, '**' = .01),
             threeparttable=TRUE,
             escape = TRUE
             
             )

coefs <- coef(uv_wmt_mnl_frame)
vcov_matrix <- vcov(uv_wmt_mnl_frame)

# Calculate the difference between coefficients
diff_against <- coefs[1, "treatment_framing_refcharity"] - coefs[1, "treatment_framing_refsolidarity"]
diff_ns <- coefs[2, "treatment_framing_refcharity"] - coefs[2, "treatment_framing_refsolidarity"]

# Standard error of the difference
se_diff_against <- sqrt(
  diag(vcov_matrix)["Against the union:treatment_framing_refcharity"] + 
    diag(vcov_matrix)["Against the union:treatment_framing_refsolidarity"] - 
    2 * vcov_matrix["Against the union:treatment_framing_refcharity", "Against the union:treatment_framing_refsolidarity"]
)

se_diff_ns <- sqrt(
  diag(vcov_matrix)["Not sure:treatment_framing_refcharity"] + 
    diag(vcov_matrix)["Not sure:treatment_framing_refsolidarity"] - 
    2 * vcov_matrix["Not sure:treatment_framing_refcharity", "Not sure:treatment_framing_refsolidarity"]
)


# Wald statistic (z-value) for the difference
z_against <- as.numeric(diff_against / se_diff_against)
z_ns <- as.numeric(diff_ns / se_diff_ns)
# p-value for the Wald test
p_against <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_against)))
p_ns <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_ns)))

Zs <- c(z_against, z_ns)
Ps <- c(p_against, p_ns)

# Display the results
test.results <- data.frame(
  Option = c("Against the union", "Not sure"),
  Z_value = Zs,
  P_value = Ps
)

# Create a nicely formatted table with kableExtra
kable(test.results, digits = 3, caption = "Testing the null that the charity and solidarity treatment effects are equal") #%>%
  #kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = FALSE)

```

# Follow-up survey (Walmart) {#app-followup-wmt}

I sent an email invitation to a followup survey to all Walmart survey respondents who provided an email.  In the end, I received `r sum(!is.na(wmt.hq$age_f))` or `r round(100*sum(!is.na(wmt.hq$age_f)) /nrow(wmt.hq))`% of those completing the main survey.

Table \@ref(tab:tab-fu-wmt) reports logistic regression estimates of selection into the followup survey based on binary and full treatment status in the main survey. There is no evidence the treatment in the main survey affected selection into the followup.

```{r tab-fu-wmt, echo = FALSE, tab.cap = "Logit regression of selection into followup", results= 'asis'}
temp<-here::here('2_code', 'Walmart', '16_followup_models_WMT.R')
source(temp)
rm(temp)

logit_tab_followup
```


In Table \@ref(tab:tab-uv-models-fu-wmt),  I report mutinomial logistic regression results for the union support question, the only outcome included in the follow up for which there was a detectable treatment effect in the main survey.   The base model compares the union vote outcomes for respondents in the followup survey based on their treatment status in the original survey.  The second model reports the same model employing stabilized IPW weights, as pre-registered.^[IPW weights were calculated using a full treatment $\times$ covariate interaction logistic regression.]  In neither case is there any detectable effect one week later, but small samples combined with the sensitivity of point estimates to the IPW weights suggests that the followup survey is too under-powered for any strong conclusions to be drawn.

# 2022 WERN survey {#app-wern}

The Worker Empowerment Research Network (WERN) fielded a survey of frontline workers in 5 industries, including retail in 2022.  Survey details and data are available at @ahlquist2022WERNWorkers2025.  Survey data have been used in several policy reports and pieces of published research, including @adams-fullerMobilizingFrontlineWorkers2025, @ahlquistRiseUnionCurious2024, and @ahlquistVoiceJobYounger2023.

Relevant to this project, the survey included a list-based question similar to Studies 1-3 in the main text. Specifically, respondents were asked about whether they had access to a series of benefits in their job.  One item in the list was  "cash aid to help in times of family emergency." The survey also included the union vote intention question as well as a set of questions about job satisfaction and quit intentions.  Covariates for age, race, gender, education, hourly pay, and job tenure are also available, enabling the specification of regressions very similar to those in the main text for job attachment and union vote intention. 

Unlike the studies reported in the main text, the "cash aid" question was the _only_ question on the survey connected in any way with EHFs.  The WERN survey does not report which retailer the respondent works for. In Studies 1-3, I am willing to call a positive response on a similar question  "pre-exposure" and "ehf awareness" because I already know whether their employer has an EHF (Studies 2 and 3) and/or I ask other questions in follow up (all three studies).  None of that exists in the WERN survey. As such, EHF measurement in the 2022 WERN survey is more tenuous and I view findings as purely supplementary.

In reporting results here, I limit the sample to currently employed non-managerial workers in retail.  We use industry weights as reported in the WERN survey.  There is no analog to the "main job" question from Studies 1-3, so that covariate is not included.  There are three job attachment indices available: one that was constructed by the WERN team independent and one I constructed based on a factor analysis of four questions (job satisfaction, employer recommendaion, attitude toward workplace attendance, and quit intentions). The quit intention question did not load heavily on the main factor, so there is a third attachment index constructed without the quit intention variable, similar to the index used in Study 2.  Estimates were directionally and inferentially identical across all three indices, so I report models using the third index as the outcome below.      

```{r tab-uv-wern, echo = FALSE, tab.cap = "Distribution of union vote intention among retail workers in the 2022 WERN survey", results= 'asis'}
wern_uv_dist_tab
```


```{r tab-uv-ja-models-wern, echo = FALSE, tab.cap = "Regressions of job attachment and union vote intention on EHF awareness among retail workers in the 2022 WERN survey", results= 'asis'}
wern_ja_ols_tab

wern_uv_mnl_tab
```
